en: *Vinaya-hṛdaya*, one fascicle.
Within the Vinaya, there are eight categories of instruction:
First, the Dharma of Training in the Precepts; Second, the Dharma of Teacher and Disciple; Third, the Dharma of the Saṃgha.

Section Four: The Method for Practicing the Path and Repenting Section Five: The Method for Practicing the Path and Cultivating Goodness Section Six: The Method for Providing Resources for the Path Section Seven: The Method for Faithful Donors and Benefactors Section Eight: The Method for Protecting and Sustaining the Dharma Treasury 1. The Method for Training in the Precepts (Śikṣāpada) The first section, the method for training in the precepts: During the twelve years following the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment...
For those of sharp faculties, he briefly established the precepts;
after twelve years, he finally entered parinirvāṇa.
For those of dull faculties who frequently committed transgressions, [he established detailed rules].
He supplemented what was deficient and rectified errors by extensively formulating the Vinaya;
it is like mending a hole in a patched robe with a square patch.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted this Vinaya Piṭaka to Upāli.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa presided over the Three Jewels and selected five hundred great arhats to compile the Dharma-piṭaka at Rājagṛha.
At that time, during a single summer retreat, Upāli ascended the high seat eighty times and fully recited the Mahāvinaya Piṭaka,
exactly as the Buddha had taught it.
This True Pure Teaching consists of eighty recitations,
all of which were entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
This Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
He entrusted this Vinaya Piṭaka to Ānanda;
and as Ānanda was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted it to two great beings:
the first was named Śāṇakavāsin.
The second is named Madhyāntika.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (Fu fazang jing),
the Venerable Madhyāntika traveled to Kaśmīra to propagate the Dharma.
This is not found in the sūtras,
nor have I seen it recorded elsewhere.
Śāṇakavāsin was traveling through the kingdom to convert others while staying in Rājagṛha.
When Śāṇakavāsin was about to pass into parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted this Dharma-treasury to Upagupta.
These are the five great masters mentioned above.
They all fully mastered the eighty thousand treasuries of the Dharma;
their wisdom and eloquence surpassed all others,
and their supernormal powers were unfathomable.
Kumāralāta had five disciples:
the first was named Sarvāstivāda,
and the second was named Mahīśāsaka.
The third was named Miśa-se;
the fourth, Bo-cou-fu-na;
and the fifth, Ka-she-wei.
These five individuals, though possessing divine understanding within the Great Canon, were incomplete in their mastery of universal penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
Furthermore, they were all sages;
observing that the ordinary beings of the final age have dull faculties and cannot fully receive the Great Vinaya Piṭaka, [they acted accordingly].
Each school has its own concise selection and rejection, differing from one another.
According to the inclinations of sentient beings, they are divided into five schools. The Buddha appeared in the world during the reign of King Zhou You;
the scriptures and images arrived during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
About one hundred years later, there was the bhikṣu Zhi Zhu,
who had a slight understanding of the Chinese language and translated the original texts of the sūtras.
When the Qin ruler Yao Xing deeply believed in the Buddha-dharma,
in the eighth year of the Hongshi era, at the Cudamani Temple (Caotang Si) in Chang’an,
the various Indian śramaṇas, including the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, [were present].
The Hu text was translated anew;
Master Kumārajīva was skilled in understanding foreign sounds and clearly comprehended the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, it was widely disseminated.

Regarding the Vinayas of the Five Schools: the first is the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya). Its master is named Sarvāstivāda; this Vinaya was recited and brought forth during the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty.
There was a Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra named Buddhayashas,
who recited the original text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and arrived at Chang’an;
together with Dharma Master Kumārajīva, he translated this Vinaya.
Before the translation of one portion was completed,
Puṇyatāra passed away. At that time,
there was the Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
Together with Dharmaruci, he continued to translate those works that had not yet been rendered.
Later, there was another Tripiṭaka Master of the Vinaya named Vimalākṣa.
This was also a text that Kumārajīva had previously sought; having come to Shouchun to seek a teacher, he stayed at Shijian Temple,
where he again collated the Vinaya text and produced three additional fascicles,
setting aside the preface to the Vinaya.
Subsequently, there were Vinayas in this land, of which the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* was the first.
Second was the *Caturvargika-vinaya*; its master was named Dharmagupta, which in this land is translated as "Dharma-rectitude."
"This person possesses the spiritual capacity of a bodhisattva and shall transmit and uphold this Vinaya.
Here in this place is the Dharma Master Zhi, a śramaṇa from the state of Jin."
He was sent westward to the land of Yuezhi,
where he obtained a copy of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* from the country of Khotan and returned to the kingdom of Qin.
In the twelfth year of the Hongshi era, the sovereign Yao Xing gathered more than three hundred śramaṇas of eminent virtue within the Chang’an temple;
these included the Qin General of Old and the Commandant of the Metropolitan Area.
The Tripiṭaka Master and Mahāyāna Vinaya Master Buddhayaśas from Kaśmīra translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Dīrgha-āgama*.
The Kuchean monk Zhu Fonian translated the Indic sounds into Chinese.
Qin Guo, Dao Yun, Dao Han, and others recorded the dictation.
This is the second part of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) concerning the flourishing of the Vinaya in this land.
Third is the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü); the name of its master of the Vinaya is Mahīśāsaka.
There was a Tripiṭaka Master and Vinaya-holder from Kaśmīra named Buddhajīva,
who respectfully brought a manuscript of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* in the Hu language to Yangzhou.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Jingping era of the Jin dynasty, the Jin Court Attendant (Shizhong) Sima Chen, Prince of Yelang,
together with the bhikṣus Zhu Daosheng, Huiyan, and others, requested that it be translated.
Fudashi has respectfully transcribed the Hu (foreign) original text without any errors.
Regarding the eastward flow of the Vinaya teachings, this is the third part of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
Fourth is the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*; the name of its master of the Vinaya is Bhadra-puṇya.
In this land there was a bhikṣu named Faxian,
who disregarded his own person and valued the Dharma;
he traveled in person to the kingdoms of the Hu to seek out and obtain Buddhist scriptures.
Arriving at the kingdom of Magadha,
he obtained a manuscript in the Hu script at the Deva Temple south of the Aśoka Stūpa in the city of Pāṭaliputra;
he then brought it back to this country.
In the eleventh month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he arrived at Yangzhou.
At Douchang Temple, he translated [this work] together with the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra.
Together with the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
these were translated from the Hu language into Chinese by the bhikṣu Baoyun;
the work was completed in its entirety in fourteen years.
The Vinaya teachings have been disseminated; this is the fourth section of the *Mahāsāṃghika*.
Fifth is the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya*, also known as the *Kāśyapīya-sūtra*;
it has not yet appeared in this land.
In the future, in the land of Han, the Vinaya Piṭaka shall have four names.
The first name shall be "Precepts" (Śīla); if translated according to the teaching, it is as follows.
The method for preventing wrongdoing is termed "precept" (śīla).
This dharma is able to restrain both body and speech.
If considered in terms of practice and understanding,
the mind that ceases evil is called precept (śīla).
This mind can control body and speech,
so that no faults may arise or be allowed to occur.
The first is called "precept" (śīla), and the second is called "discipline" (vinaya). If translated according to the meaning of the teaching,
that which evaluates the gravity of offenses is termed "discipline."
If translated according to its function, it tames those who are stubborn and unruly;
thus it is called "Vinaya" (Discipline). Its three names, beginning with "Prātimokṣa," are transliterations of the Indic language.
In Chinese, these are called "various liberations.
If translated according to the meaning of the teaching,
this refers to the method for untying bonds.
If one relies [on this] to go forth as a renunciant, being unhindered wherever one may be, both body and mind will be non-active; therefore it is called "liberation in each and every instance.
If translated according to its practice:
The mind that severs its bonds is able to separate itself from afflictions moment by moment;
therefore, it is called "liberation in each and every instance. The fourth name, *vinaya*, is likewise a Western [Indic] term.
In this region, it is called "extinguishing.
If translated according to the teaching,
this dharma can thoroughly pacify disputes and arguments.
Therefore, it is called "cessation.
If translated according to its function,
it means the severing and elimination of birth and death.
The exhaustion of suffering is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
tranquility and detachment constitute cessation (*nirodha*). Among these four, the first two are designated according to their causes:
that which externally guards [the senses] is called morality (*śīla*).
The first is named according to its internal conformity with the precepts; the latter two are named according to their results.
Liberation (*vimukti*) is the state where afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted.
This is the fruit of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. That which is "extinction" (*nirodha*)—wherein both body and wisdom are exhausted—is the fruit of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, both precepts (*śīla*) and discipline (*vinaya*) serve as the cause that penetrates to the fruit.
This is the conditioned practice of transcendence;
liberation and cessation are its results, which encompass both cause and effect.
This is the unconditioned practice of renunciation.
Regarding why these four are all called "Pitakas" (baskets):
if explained in terms of the teachings,
they are named "Pitaka" because their textual content and underlying meaning are richly comprehensive.
If explained according to its function,
it is called a "treasury" (kośa) because it gives rise to manifold virtues and brings forth inexhaustible benefit.
Next, the method for receiving the precepts is explained.
Regarding the five methods of receiving the precepts:
the position for receiving the precepts through the "superior method" (ūrdhvadharma) lies at or above the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This applies to a person who has attained arhatship.
This is called receiving the full ordination (upasampadā).
Because the Tathāgata attained the Way, realized perfect enlightenment, and fully verified the principle without awakening through a teacher, he is said to have "naturally" obtained the precepts.
If disciples all receive them through their own vow, [they likewise obtain them].
The Buddhas serve as witnesses;
because one attains the most supreme Dharma, it is called "receiving the precepts of the superior Dharma" (adhi-dharma-śīla).
Within this, two [aspects] are contained.
The two types of "welcoming" (svāgata) ordination—by nature and by self-vow—are positions for those who have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna or higher.
Such individuals, riding upon the roots of goodness from previous lives, come to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Having explained the Four Noble Truths, the path was established for the attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
She sought refuge and left the household life;

by the Holy One’s command, "Come, Bhikṣuṇī," she immediately attained full ordination. This is known as receiving the precepts through the "Come-hither" (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*) formula. This is the method of receiving the precepts from the three masters. A woman may also attain this, provided she constantly guards against the possibility of regression.
Seeking compassion, she requested to leave the household life;
the Tathāgata taught her the Eight Rules of Respect and dispatched Ānanda to transmit them to her.
They were commanded to honor and follow the Great Sangha as their teachers and models;

upon receiving the instructions, they immediately attained full ordination, which is called "ordination by the 'Come-hither' (ehi-bhikṣu) formula. The stage of ordination received through the three or four statements belongs to the level of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and above.
This person encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world,
yet heard [the Dharma] without seeing him;
a certain arhat then conferred the Three Refuges upon him.

Because it involves the formal utterance of the complete formula, it is called "receiving the precepts through three statements. The stage of receiving the precepts through five *karmavācanās* extends down to those who are still ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*).
Such individuals have weak and meager roots of goodness, and it is difficult for the mind of the Way to arise in them.

It requires the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) performed by a quorum of ten monks to be completed before one attains full ordination; therefore, it is called "receiving the precepts through *karma*.
Furthermore, it necessitates the presence of six causal conditions.
Only then can one fully receive the precepts:
first, the person receiving the precepts must not have the thirteen obstacles;
second, they must be twenty years of age.
The three robes and alms bowl are complete; the preceptor and the assembly of monks are full and pure according to the Dharma.
Fifth, [the candidate] is within the boundary (sīmā) and not separated from the group by the limits of their respective spheres.

Sixth, the formal ritual consisting of one motion (jñapti) and three proclamations (karmavācanā), along with its preliminary and subsequent procedures, is complete in both wording and phrasing. Within the *Mātṛkā* there are ten ways of receiving the precepts.
There are five kinds of bhikṣus:
first, those by way of the higher dharma;
second, those who have come well (svāgata).
Third, the threefold proclamation;
fourth, the command to listen;
fifth, the formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*).
There are also five kinds of *bhikṣuṇīs*:
first, those by the True Dharma;
second, those by "Come Hither" (*svāgata*).
1. The Dharma of the Three Preceptors;
2. Sending a Messenger;
3. The Karmavācanā.
These constitute ten types.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* clarifies ten methods for receiving the precepts.
The first is attaining the precepts naturally.
This refers to the Buddha, who attained self-awakening without a teacher;
second, those who obtained the precepts through a self-vow, such as Mahākāśyapa.
Third, obtaining the precepts through the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*),
meaning that the five bhikṣus, beginning with Kauṇḍinya, immediately attained full ordination upon hearing the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
Fourth, obtaining the precepts through the "Come hither" formula (*ehibhikṣu*).
This refers to Yaśas and others, as well as those whom the Tathāgata converted through the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu) formula throughout his lifetime.
Why is this? Because the Buddha is the Dharma King and personally conferred the precepts upon them;
furthermore, these were their final existences, and they never again had to study the impermanence of the stages [of training].
Fifth is the attainment of the precepts through the threefold formula.
This refers to those ordained by Arhats prior to the establishment of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures),
who attained full ordination simply by receiving the three refuges.
Sixth, obtaining the precepts through question and answer,
which is also called "discussing the meaning.
This refers to the novice Śudāya, who was only seven years old at the time.
The Buddha questioned him on the meaning of these points,
and he answered each one.
The Buddha, approving of his responses with a noble mind, commanded the bhikṣus to grant him full ordination.
It is named after the question-and-answer session;
thus it is called "obtaining the precepts through questioning.
Because it was due to the command given to the bhikṣus, it is also called "obtaining the precepts through being commanded to listen."
Seventh are the eight respects through which one obtains the precepts;
these are also called the "eight kinds" and are further referred to as the "eight rules of reverence for the teacher."
It is also called the "Eight Rules Not to Be Transgressed.
This refers to when Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred Śākya women requested ordination from the Buddha;
the Buddha sent Ānanda to confer upon them the Eight Respectful Rules, and having agreed to them, they were granted ordination.
It is named after the Eight Respectful Precepts;
therefore, it is called "obtaining the precepts through the Eight Respects.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Having received the eight rules from Ānanda, Māyādevī joyfully accepted them upon the crown of her head.
She then said to Ānanda, "Please inform the Buddha on my behalf."
Among these eight rules, please grant me one further request:
allow the bhikṣuṇīs to pay respects to the bhikṣus according to their seniority. [The Buddha said:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old pay respects to a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If I were to permit bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to bhikṣus according to their seniority,
such a thing would be impossible."
Having heard this, Ānanda returned and reported it to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said, "To receive [the teaching] upon the crown of my head with reverence and joyfully practice it is itself called 'leaving the household life' and 'receiving the full ordination. She then spoke again to Ānanda.
"What should these five hundred Śākya women do now? Let them speak to the Buddha on my behalf.
The Buddha said, "I grant that Mahāprajāpatī shall serve as their preceptor (upādhyāyī)."

Within the assembly of ten bhikṣus, when receiving the precepts through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman), it is permitted for the ritual to be performed simultaneously for three persons; it must not reach four, yet this is permissible.
This is how Mahāprajāpatī alone received the precepts under the eight weighty rules (gurudharma).
The five hundred Śākya women then received the precepts through *karmavācanā*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise.
If one follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the five hundred Śākya women also all obtained the precepts by means of the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
Eighth is obtaining the precepts through the dispatching of a messenger.
This refers to the case of the courtesan Upacālā, whose countenance was so beautiful that her departure from the monastery would have caused obstacles to the violation of the conduct [of the monks].
The Noble One granted permission for one bhikṣuṇī to act as a messenger among the great assembly of monks to receive the precepts on her behalf; therefore,
this is called "receiving the precepts by dispatching a messenger."
Receiving the precepts through the ninefold *karmavācanā* refers to the ritual procedure performed by a quorum of ten monks;
this is the practice for maintaining the Vinaya in the border regions.
The five men received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Because the Buddha-dharma was only beginning to spread in this borderland,
the monastic community was extremely sparse, making it difficult to assemble the required number.
Therefore, the Great Sage opened the way for the five men to receive the precepts.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who has attained arhatship is immediately called one who has gone forth and received full ordination."
This person attains the most excellent dharma, which is called receiving the precepts of the supreme dharma (*uttama-dharma*).
Thus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"At that time, there was one whose age was less than twenty."
However, upon receiving the precepts, a doubt arose regarding the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to calculate the months spent in the womb as well as the intercalary months; even with these added, [the time] is still not yet full."
The Buddha asked,
"Does this person attain arhatship?
He replied:
"It is permitted.

The Buddha said, "This person is called one who has received the full ordination in the highest manner. Furthermore, among the community of nuns, a woman who was twelve years old at the time of her marriage is permitted to receive the full precepts."
In total, there are twelve ways of receiving the precepts.
Among these twelve, only the Buddha alone attained the precepts spontaneously (*svayaṃ-prāpta*).
Only Mahākāśyapa alone attained the precepts through his own vow (*svayaṃ-pratijñāta*).
It is seen that receiving the precepts through "seeing the Emperor" was restricted to the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya;
whereas receiving the precepts through the "Come hither" formula applied universally to both monks and nuns.

During the Buddha's lifetime, there were those who received the Dharma by this means, but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were no longer any such instances of receiving the Dharma through the "Come hither" formula.

Receiving the precepts through the threefold formula is restricted to the Great Bhikṣu-saṃgha; it was permitted prior to the establishment of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), but is not permitted thereafter.
Receiving the precepts through question and answer is restricted to the *śrāmaṇera* Sūdāya.
If, in the present age of the Final Dharma, there are śrāmaṇeras such as Śudāya, they are likewise permitted to receive the precepts;
however, the attainment of the eight weighty rules (gurudharma) is restricted exclusively to the female community, specifically to the single individual, Mahāprajāpatī.
It does not apply to others;
the delegation of authority to bestow the precepts applies only to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, specifically to the Bhikṣuṇīs of Vārāṇasī.
However, it is also permitted for such Bhikṣuṇīs to do so in this present degenerate age.
A small countenance cannot be tolerated.
Therefore, the five men of the borderlands attained the precepts;
now, the Buddha-dharma exists in the frontier regions.
All initial practices are permitted;
those who have previously married are restricted to the twelve categories within the community of nuns;
and the formal reception of the higher ordination is open to both the communities of monks and nuns.
Now, if there are those who have attained Arhatship, they are likewise said to have received the "Higher Dharma Ordination" (uttarimanussa-sīla).
Only the single method of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is a teaching common to both ordinary beings and noble ones, extending to both monks and nuns.

One must understand that the efficacy of the ritual procedures for both present and future [practitioners] depends on whether they are successfully accomplished; this shall be explained extensively according to the various schools (*nikāya*). Question:
How many conditions must be fulfilled for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) to be designated as "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*)? Answer:
According to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, six causes and conditions must be fulfilled for an act to be considered in accordance with the Dharma. What are these six?
First, the person receiving the precepts must be at least twenty-three years of age and possess both robes and bowl.
Second, the person receiving the precepts must be free from the thirteen impediments.
Third, it is essential that the boundary (sīmā) be duly established.
Fourth, the entire Saṃgha within the boundary has assembled without any separate groups.
Fifth, the *karmavācanā* is recited without addition or omission.
Sixth, ten monks are present, complete and pure according to the Dharma.
When these six conditions are complete, one is said to have received the precepts in accordance with the Dharma.
If even one of these six is lacking, the reception of the precepts is not accomplished. Question:
What is meant by "having reached the age of twenty"? Answer:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One must be twenty years of age;
being twenty years of age is equivalent to being twenty *li* [in stature]."
If one is both twenty years old and not yet twenty, one cannot receive the precepts;
however, if both conditions are fulfilled, one may receive them.
If one is born in winter and receives the precepts at the conclusion of the summer retreat, [one is considered to have reached the required age].
This is called being less than twenty years of age.
If one is born during the spring season and receives the precepts after the summer retreat has concluded,
this is called being less than twenty years of age.
If one is born during the period of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), they receive the precepts upon the conclusion of the preceding *varṣā*;
if one is born during the period of the subsequent *varṣā*, they receive the precepts upon the conclusion of that subsequent *varṣā*.
This is called being "full twenty years."
The Dharmaguptaka school reckons twelve months as one year;
when twenty years are complete, counting from the month of birth, they are all said to have reached twenty and may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The Mahāsāṃghika school requires that twenty years be completed by the end of both [the lunar and solar] cycles before one may receive full ordination.
For example, one born in the twelfth month who reaches twenty years of age only after having passed eighteen lunar months is called "not yet full" [twenty];
likewise, these [requirements] necessitate being full twenty *varṣa*s (rainy seasons).
Only then can one receive the precepts.
Since the matter of receiving the precepts is weighty and constitutes the very foundation of renunciation,
if the original rite is not accomplished, one is not a bhikṣu.
To be no different from laypeople in receiving the faithful offerings of others and in accepting their prostrations is called stealing; one incurs immeasurable guilt.
If a person knows for certain that another has received the precepts at a young age,
then even if a hundred years have passed, that person remains like a śrāmaṇera;
they should not receive the prostrations of a great bhikṣu, nor should they accept offerings from the faithful.
Regarding the Re-ordination: Question.
Since this person has already undergone ordination and has fully participated in the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* ceremonies, for what reason may they receive the precepts again? Answer.
This person intends to receive the full ordination;
they listen to the *karmavācanā* and the *poṣadha*,
and it is not out of a thieving mind.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) permits receiving the precepts again.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Monǐ jīlü) states: "If a person does not know their age, one should ask their parents, relatives, or neighbors."
If one still does not know, one should consult the birth-year board (*janmapatra*).
If that is unavailable, one should observe whether his facial features and limbs are well-proportioned. If one still does not know by these means, [one should resort to other methods].
One should ask which king reigned in which year, and whether the land was abundant or in scarcity, or subject to drought or flood; this does not mean that all such matters must be known.
If there are times when these things are difficult to know, one should investigate each point individually; if, after such investigation, one truly does not know, [one should remain silent].
Even if one has completed twenty years and possesses full hands and feet, one still does not obtain the precepts. Question:
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Those who have not yet reached twenty years of age are permitted [to receive ordination]."
Regarding the calculation of months spent in the womb, intercalary months, and so forth—how is this further explained? Answer:
There are those who, at the time of first receiving the precepts, intend that they shall receive them once they have reached twenty years of age.
Only then did he realize his calculation was incomplete and, harboring doubts, he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said,
"I permit you to count the months spent in the womb and to include intercalary months."
If one recites the *Poṣadha* every fourteen days throughout the entire year,
there is no offense for one who has completed the full number of years.
This is the Great Sage’s opening of the rule, by which one obtains the precepts through the combination [of days].
According to the laws of this country, an intercalary month is added every five years;
however, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that King Bimbisāra added an intercalary month once every six years.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* [states] that there is one intercalary month every five years;
it is not yet known upon what basis this is fixed. Question:
Is it possible to receive the precepts without possessing a robe and bowl?
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who lacks a robe and bowl may not receive the precepts. It further asks:
"May one receive the precepts by borrowing a robe and bowl? The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: [the same].
One who borrows robes should be instructed by the owner of the robes to relinquish them so that they may receive the precepts. The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Can one obtain the precepts without a robe and bowl?
The answer is: "Yes, one can."
If that is so, what need is there for robes and alms bowls?
He replied: "Firstly, it is for the sake of proper deportment."
Second, it is for the sake of generating merit in those who have passed away;
third, it is because one must possess both robes and bowl to manifest the distinctive marks [of a monk].
Second, regarding the absence of impediments or disqualifications in one's person:
Why must this be asked? Answer:
Because the thirteen difficult cases are dragged away by the three obstacles;
being separated from the Noble Path, these obstacles prevent the arising of the precepts.
It is called "difficult" (duskarāḥ).
Therefore, one must inquire. Furthermore, it is asked:
what are the names and meanings of the thirteen difficulties? The answer is as follows:
First is the offense that is difficult to atone for:
this person once received the full precepts,
but having committed a *pārājika* offense, was expelled from the Saṃgha.
Thereafter, he again sought to leave the household life;
however, because he was excluded from the assembly and termed a "border-impediment" (pratyantika) who could not receive the precepts, it is called a "difficulty.
Second is the difficulty of defiling a nun’s pure conduct.
One who has not committed sexual misconduct since going forth is said to be of pure conduct.
If one was defiled while still a layperson, such a person is not considered difficult [to ordain]. Third is the difficulty of receiving the precepts with a thievish mind.
This person shaves his hair and beard and dons the kāṣāya robe without a teacher;
though he does not receive the precepts, he participates in the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* rituals, and because he thus steals the Buddha-dharma, he is called one with a "thief's mind."

If one of the three lower groups of practitioners listens to the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts while stealing [the opportunity], or falsely pretends to participate in the affairs of the Saṃgha, they also commit an offense. This is the fourth difficulty regarding the breaking of internal and external paths:
such a person was formerly an outsider who has come [to the Saṃgha].

After having left the household life and received the precepts, if one does not abandon them but returns to enter among the non-Buddhists, and because of the weight of their wrong views naturally loses the precepts, yet wishes again to seek to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha-dharma—this is called a "difficulty. Fifth is the difficulty of being a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*); such a person has many afflictions and is deficient [in faculties].
Regarding the difficulty of observing the precepts:
because the afflictions and hindrances are heavy, one does not give rise to the Great Precepts;
therefore, it is called a "difficulty. Sixth, the difficulty of killing one's father; seventh, the difficulty of killing one's mother.
8. Killing one’s father or mother as a layperson (śuklāmbaram) constitutes a grave violation of gratitude that obstructs the arising of the precepts. 9. Killing an Arhat;
for instance, killing a bhikṣu while he was still a layperson, such that his complexion did not change at the moment of death. 10. Causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
To forget and preach false dharmas, or to confuse the minds of the multitude;

to perform separate religious rites within the same realm, thereby severing and destroying the Buddha-dharma—knowingly and intentionally doing so is called a "difficulty. Tenth is the difficulty of shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
This person, through their contrivance, intended to kill the Buddha but was unable to take his life;
yet, by injuring the holy body, they committed a grave offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya) due to their violation of the fundamental principle.
In this present age of the final dharma, if one destroys monasteries, images, or relics, or even sees an auspicious sign [of such destruction], one incurs the grave offense of逆罪 (ānantarya-karma).
Because one cannot receive the precepts [under such conditions], it is called a "difficulty. Eleventh is the difficulty of non-human beings (amanuṣya).
If a ghost or a deity transforms into human form with the intent to receive the full precepts, this is called the "obstacle of non-humans. Twelve is the "obstacle of animals":
if a dragon or a fox transforms into human form.

One must not confer the precepts upon them. Regarding the thirteenth obstacle of having both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjanaka*): such a person possesses both male and female organs within a single body and finds no place within either of the two communities, that of the monks or the nuns.
Therefore, they are called "difficult.
Among these thirteen types of persons,
the first four and those with the karmic obstruction of the five heinous crimes are subsumed under the category of karmic obstruction.
The one eunuch is subsumed under the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the latter three are subsumed under the retributive hindrance (*vipākāvaraṇa*). They are thus encompassed by the three hindrances.
Within a single form, it cannot be altered.
If one has not yet left the household life, do not ordain them;
if they have already left the household life, you should cause them to cease [their practice].
A detailed explanation is as set forth in the treatise. Question:
It was not asked whether one obtains the precepts through the thirteen difficulties. Answer:
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Having already restrained oneself, one does not obtain the precepts. He asked again:
"Originally, this was for the purpose of preventing difficulties;
since there are currently no such [difficulties], why is it necessary to ask? He replied:
Although you ask because it is difficult,
if there were truly a difficulty in asking,
one would not obtain the precepts in either case— whether by asking or by not asking.
If there are truly no difficulties or objections, one obtains the precepts;
if one does not inquire [about such matters], one does not obtain the precepts. Third, the establishment of the boundary (sīmā) is clarified;
this will be explained later in the section on the method for establishing a boundary. Fourth, the entire Saṃgha assembles within the boundary.

Those who do not come must grant their consent; thus the Sangha remains in harmony, without a schism. Regarding the fifth *karmavācanā*, as for the wording of the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the fourfold proclamation (*karmavācanā*):
if one performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Furthermore, if there are five, three, two, or one [monks] who recite the *jñapti*, none of these are valid. Regarding the sixth requirement, the completion of the number of monks:
it requires ten pure, fully ordained (*bhikṣu*) monks.
If there are more than ten people, it is called a full assembly;
if fewer, it is not accomplished. Question:
If one who has committed a grave offense or one of the thirteen types of persons with impediments acts as an upādhyāya...
"Does this count toward obtaining the precepts? Answer:
The *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states:
"This does not suffice for the quorum of the Saṃgha."
One does not obtain the precepts. As for the remaining witnesses, if they commit a grave offense, it matters only that there be many witnesses so that one obtains the precepts;
if there are few, one does not obtain the precepts.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
At that time, there was one who had not maintained the precepts;
after receiving the full ordination from his preceptor, he gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"Do you know that your preceptor does not uphold the precepts?
He replied:
"I know. Do you know that one should not follow such a person?
Would such a person receive full ordination?"
He replied,
"I do not know.
The Buddha said:
This is called receiving the full precepts. Furthermore, there was one who gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Do you know whether your preceptor has broken the precepts?"
He replied,
"I know. You know that you should not follow [this]."
"Is one permitted to receive the precepts from a person who has broken the precepts? He replied,
"I know."
The Buddha said,
"Do you know that one cannot receive the precepts from a person who has broken the precepts?
He replied:
"I do not know.
The Buddha said, "He is considered to have received full ordination. Regarding the fourth person, who knows all three phrases:
The Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination. Question:
"Can one receive full ordination without a preceptor?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Upāli asked: [The Buddha replied: "It is not permitted."
"Can one receive full ordination without a preceptor?
The Buddha said,
"One may be said to have received full ordination."
Regarding the *karmavācanā* officiant and the assembly of monks having offenses: The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
At that time, there was an upādhyāya who conferred full ordination upon a nine-year-old person.
He did not know whether the precepts had been successfully established.
The Buddha said,
"The reception of the precepts is accomplished;
however, the Saṃgha has committed an offense."
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the preceptor does not complete the number of ten persons, one is not said to have received full ordination. Moreover, one does not announce one's own name, nor does one announce the name of the preceptor.
If one does not request the precepts, it is in no way called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there were those who were not given the śrāmaṇera precepts, yet were immediately granted full ordination."
"Is it not known whether the receiving of the precepts has been accomplished? The Buddha said, "They have obtained full ordination.
Regarding the transgressions of the Saṃgha, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
At that time, there was one who had received the precepts from a teacher of broken discipline;
he gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should know this first:
did your preceptor receive the precepts from his own teacher?
He replied:
"I do not know.
The Buddha said, "It is called receiving the precepts. Question: [What is meant by this?]
Can the Great Sangha confer the six dharmas and the ten precepts upon a bhikṣuṇī? Answer:
The Great Sangha may only perform three types of *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣuṇī:
first, the conferral of the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Second is *mānāpya*; third is the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
Regarding other ritual matters, there are no textual accounts in the various Vinayas.
Even if the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the performer is not accomplished, both the monk and the nun incur an offense. Question:
For what reason does a *mahābhikṣuṇī* take a bhikṣu as her preceptor?
The śikṣamāṇā does not take [the precepts] alone. The answer is:
women lack the resolve for solitude;
therefore, the Sage established the requirement to receive the full ordination.
One must take a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) as one's preceptor.
As for a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*) or a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*), at the beginning of their renunciation, during their first year, and when their resolve is still weak,
they rely solely on a fully ordained nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) as their preceptor.
Question: When receiving the training precepts (*śikṣā*), is it necessary to have a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) present? Answer: No. Question:
When receiving the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharmāḥ*), is it further necessary to request a preceptor (*upādhyāya*)? Answer: No.
It is not necessary. Why is this so?
Because a śikṣamāṇā merely adds the training in six [precepts] to the ten precepts.
Since this is not yet a case of changing one's position, there is no need to request [permission].
Furthermore, all four divisions of the Vinaya state that it refers to a place where one can see with the eyes but cannot hear with the ears.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) while facing [the recipient], the reception is not accomplished;
one incurs an offense regarding the six rules. Question:
Some say that a *bhikṣuṇī* may perform prostrations to a *śrāmaṇera*.
"Is this in accordance with the Dharma? He replied, "This person does not understand the characteristics of the Vinaya;
he speaks thus falsely."
Why is this? Because in the *Vastu-varga* (Chapter on Dwellings) of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*,
the Buddha himself established the rules for veneration for the sake of the bhikṣus.
A novice monk (śrāmaṇera) should pay homage to a senior novice nun (śrāmaṇerī);
how much more so should he pay homage to a senior bhikṣuṇī? Who are those to whom one should not pay homage?

Those who have committed one of the thirteen grave offenses (trayodaśa-ānantarya), those who have been formally censured three times (tri-ud-dhura), those who have undergone the funeral rites (nirvāpaṇa), and those who speak what is contrary to the Dharma (adharma-vādī).
Persons such as these should not be venerated;

those who do so incur offense both for themselves and the other. Next, the renunciation of the precepts is explained: however, the precepts are a pure dharma that ought to ascend clearly above all burdens.
Therefore, the fivefold assembly of monks and nuns must protect and uphold the Buddha’s precepts;
they would rather die than transgress them.
If one should intentionally violate them, it is no different from never having left the household life in the first place.
For what reason?
Because they destroy the Dharma of the Path themselves and bring disgrace upon their teachers and the Sangha.
They defile and bring disorder to the Triple Gem;
they deceive and wrong the Fourfold Benefactors;
failing to digest the offerings of the faithful, they only increase their transgressions.
This is especially prevalent.
If a person’s mind is oppressed by afflictions and their aspiration for the Path is thin,
such that they wish to commit evil and cannot restrain themselves;
The Buddha said,
"Such a person may be permitted to renounce the precepts and return home; however, they must not rely upon the Buddha-dharma to violate the pure prohibitions."
If one wishes to relinquish the precepts,
one should kneel with both knees on the ground and join the palms before a single bhikṣu,
speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name],
now relinquish the great precepts."
I have returned to being a layperson.
May the Venerable One remember that I am now a layperson.
Thus it is said three times. Furthermore, within the reception of the precepts, there is both *vijñapti* (informative action) and *avijñapti* (non-informative action).
Initially, one forms the intention to receive the precepts in the presence of a teacher;
through the movement of body and speech, this dharma is brought to completion.
Therefore, it is called "active precept" (*vijñapti-śīla*).
After the precepts have been obtained, one maintains them within the mind and no longer engages in further [physical] activity; therefore, it is called "non-active precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*).
This non-active precept is a supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*).
If one intentionally accepts it, one gains [the result];
if one intentionally abandons it, one loses the wholesome karma.
Otherwise, it will inevitably bring about its fruit.
There is no sense of relinquishment;
this differs from the precepts, which possess the sense of relinquishment.
Regarding the five categories of precepts, the act of receiving them was explained above.
Now, to clarify the observance of the precepts:
having already received and understood the principles of the Dharma,
one must protect and maintain them by restraining the mind according to circumstances so as not to commit transgressions.
Offenses vary in gravity and are ranked into five levels;
these categories follow one another in sequence, forming this chapter. "Pārājika" is a transliteration of a Western (Sanskrit) term.
This is called "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*).
If one violates this precept, one is forever cast out from the pure assembly; therefore, it is called "without remainder.
One shall not be included in the two types of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*): the *poṣadha* and the *karmavācanā*.

Because there is forever no portion [of the original state] remaining, it is called "without remainder" (anavaśeṣa). Second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* precepts—this is translated as "monastic residue" (*sengcan*).
If one commits such an offense, one's conduct becomes impaired and deficient; one is no longer fit [to remain in the community].
Regarding the number of *poṣadha* [observances], they are excluded from the assembly for *karmavācanā*;
because their nature is similar [to that of a formal act], they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The three *pāyattika* precepts are translated in this region as "falling" (*duo*).

If one violates this precept, one falls into hell; because one is scorched, boiled, and obstructed, it is called "falling. These are the four *pāyattika* (or *pratideśanīya*) precepts, which in this land are translated as "confessing to another."
If one violates these precepts, the matter is subject to censure;

however, because it is permitted for one to confess and purify the offense before another person, it is said that "one should repent before them. These five *śikṣāpada* rules are translated here as "matters that should be studied."
Dignified deportment and refined practice are only perfected through the diligent cultivation of the precepts;
therefore it is said that one should train in these five categories of offenses by guarding three types of conduct.
Among them, the first category guards fundamental conduct.
The second section concerns the practice of protecting the assembly;
the following three sections concern the practice of protecting dignified deportment.
Furthermore, these five sections prevent three kinds of obstacles.
The first two sections prevent offenses that obstruct the Path.
The first section [the *pārājika*] directly obstructs the Path;
the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* directly obstructs the Saṃgha.
The first section of the *Pāyattika* prevents the transgression of causing others to undergo retribution;
[otherwise,] one would sink into the three realms of existence with no means of escape.
The latter two sections prevent the transgressions of contemptuous speech and excessive fault-finding.
If one fails to skillfully transform and benefit those who have not yet been born [into the path], it is improper.
Regarding the *Tissaṇīya* (Pāyantika) offenses, once one has committed an offense, one must encourage [the offender] to repent.
Below, one should study with diligence; the meaning of "offense" applies generally across all categories.
This is merely to manifest the Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, the five categories were established in order to prevent the offenses of the five grades.
The Buddha said:
To repent with a guilty mind is what is prevented by the fifth category [of offenses].
To repent of a transgression before another is [the practice prescribed].
This refers to what is prohibited by the fourth category [of offenses].
An offense that is minor yet grave must also be confessed before another;
this refers to what is prohibited by the third category.
There are grave offenses that are expiated through confession before the Sangha;
these are the matters prevented by the second category [of the Prātimokṣa].
There are also most grave offenses that cannot be expiated.
This refers to what is prevented by the first category [of offenses].
The first category prevents crimes punishable by death; the second category prevents crimes punishable by near-death penalties;
and the third category prevents crimes for which one would otherwise receive lashes.
The fourth category prevents the offense of receiving a staff;
the fifth category prevents the offense of spitting and losing [food].
These five categories of precepts all take the cessation of unwholesome conduct through body and speech as their essence.
Because it branches out into five categories, it is called the "fivefold" (pañcāṅga).
Among the various precepts, those of the initial section are called the "precepts of fundamental action-purity.
The second category is called the "precepts of subsequent and antecedent subsidiary purity."
The third chapter is titled "The Precept of Purifying Awareness by Means of Non-evil Cognitions.
The fourth chapter is "The Precept of Purifying Mindfulness through Guarding Right Mindfulness.
The fifth chapter is titled "The Precept of Dedication toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras: "Śrāmaṇera" is a Sanskrit term;
here it is translated as "Cessation and Compassion.
Because they cease evil and practice compassion, they are called śrāmaṇeras.
One receives the ten precepts precisely because one ceases the ten unwholesome actions;
because of compassionate mindfulness toward sentient beings, there arise the prohibitions against killing and so forth.
These ten precepts are the very foundation of all precepts.
First, regarding the observance of the precepts: (1) one must not kill; if one intentionally kills a human being, one shall not receive the precepts.
If one kills animals or the like, one may extinguish that transgression by repenting with a sincere heart. (2) One must not steal; whether it be thievery, robbery, or forcible seizure.
If one burns or damages another's property, even if it is worth only five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, one shall not receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

If the value is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, or if the object belongs to non-humans or animals, one may extinguish the offense through repentance. However, if the object belongs to a human male or female, [the case is different].
If they are non-human males or females,
or animals of either sex,
or if their physical bodies have been violated, they may not receive the full precepts.

If one touches [a woman] and so forth, it can be extinguished by repenting with a sincere mind. Fourth, regarding false speech: if one falsely claims to have attained the state of an *ārya*, one shall not receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, if one slanders a pure person with grave charges, or deceives and misleads others through falsehoods.

The transgression of this [lying] is difficult to repent for; other minor false speech may be forgiven once repentance has been performed, after which one may proceed to the higher precepts. Fifth, do not drink alcohol:
the nature of alcohol can give rise to great afflictions, alter one's mental disposition, and disturb the path-mind of humanity.
It opens many doors for various transgressions;
if alcohol enters the belly, the mind that guards the precepts becomes lax,
and because self-restraint can no longer be maintained, [transgressions follow].

6. One should strictly guard against taking intoxicating drugs. 7. One must not wear flower garlands, smear the body with fragrant oils, or adorn oneself with flowery finery out of a fondness for such things;

nor should one harbor deep attachment within, which may disturb the Path. 8. One must not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor go to watch or listen to them, nor associate with those who indulge in such frivolous amusements and license.

If one’s body and speech are externally unrestrained and dissolute, and the mind for the Way is floating and scattered—(8) sitting upon a high or broad bed with an air of arrogance and self-importance, lacking a humble heart—one exists in a state that deceives others;
such a person is far removed from the Way. (9) One must not eat at improper times; to sustain life and nourish the Way, one should act in accordance with the Dharma.

Indulging in flavors without moderation leads to affliction and obstructs the Path; tenth, one should not handle raw gold, silver, precious objects, or articles for personal use—frugality and simplicity are best.
Precious ornaments and finery give rise to much greed and contention.
Therefore, the teaching prohibits grasping. Among these ten [precepts], the first four are grave by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), while the latter six are grave by prohibition (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
Those that are grave by nature involve the arising of evil within oneself.
Regarding the prevention of gravity: externally, it prevents the arising of evil.

Furthermore, the first four precepts are the four precepts within the category of the purity of action (*karmapariśuddhi-śīla*), while these [remaining ones] constitute the purity of conduct (*caryāpariśuddhi-śīla*).
The latter two precepts constitute the precept of purity through conditions.
Why is this? Because regarding the two precepts against killing and stealing, one neither performs them oneself nor instructs others to do so.
Thus, both body and speech are pure:
the single precept against sexual misconduct ensures the purity of bodily action alone,
while the single precept against false speech ensures the purity of verbal action alone.
Not killing is to be free from the mind of anger;
not stealing is to be free from external greed;
not committing sexual misconduct is to be free from internal greed.
By abstaining from false speech, one leaves behind the delusion of wrong views and the mind of folly;
by uprooting the three poisons, the mental karma is purified.
The foundation of pure precepts gives rise to the purification of the karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, it is said that the first four precepts are merely the precept of purity of action (*karmaviśuddhi-śīla*).
Since one wishes to initiate practice based on action,
one must first protect against transgressions.
One abstains from drinking alcohol so that various evils do not arise;
since evil has not arisen,
one should next cultivate and refine one's deportment.
Because his deportment is refined and pure, and he is free from worldly defilements,
he next does not wear flower garlands or anoint his body with fragrant oils.
His deportment having been thus established, [the text continues].
Next, one should exercise the body and mouth by chanting verses of the sublime Dharma, seeking out virtuous friends to inquire about and receive teachings not yet heard.

Yet, on the contrary, you sigh and spit upon what is not the Dharma, stirring up the emotions of the masses, specializing only in secular arts, listening for and gathering strange anomalies, abandoning the correct to pursue the heterodox, and maintaining conduct that deviates from the patterns of the Way. Therefore—
Next, one should not engage in singing, dancing, or performing arts, nor intentionally go to watch or listen to them.
Once one has finished listening and practicing, one should then properly settle the mind,
applying oneself with diligence to the Dharma and maintaining focused mindfulness.
To subdue pride, endure honor and disgrace,
and remain free from laxity, indulgence, and self-indulgence.
Next, one should not sit upon a high or wide bed;
therefore it is said that the four intermediate precepts constitute the practice of pure morality.
However, the Way does not arise in isolation; its practice arises in dependence upon conditions.
Food and drink sustain life;
clothing protects the body.
It is only through the support of both internal and external necessities that one is able to practice the Way.
Next, one does not eat at improper times nor wear precious ornaments,
thereby distancing oneself from the faults of attachment to the requisites for life.
Therefore, it is said that the latter two precepts are the "precepts of purity regarding conditions."

Observing the precepts brings ten benefits: first, one is included within the Saṅgha; if those of lower rank observe the precepts, they constitute a community that accords with the Dharma and are counted among its members.

Second, it causes the Saṅgha to rejoice; if those of middle rank observe the precepts, whatever they undertake will delight the hearts of the assembly. Third, it brings peace and happiness to the Saṅgha; if those of higher rank observe the precepts, they will adorn the communal observances with splendor.

Furthermore, he can provide shelter and benefit to his disciples in four ways: first, he causes those who have not yet had faith to believe; second, his precepts and virtue are fully prepared within, so that outwardly he inspires the faith and respect of others, making him fit to serve as a teacher and model;
third, people rely upon him to save the world.
For this reason, those who have not yet left the household life come to believe in and delight in leaving the household life, and they receive the precepts from him.
Fifth, having already gained faith, he causes it to increase and expand; once he has ordained disciples, he is further able to instruct and admonish them.

Sixth, to cause those who are difficult to tame to become disciplined: if among the assembly there are those of evil nature, who are unruly, disobedient to instructions, transgressors of prohibitions, or who do not conform to dignified decorum, [the teacher] shall cause them to be tamed.

Furthermore, one is able to punish and subdue according to the Dharma to bring about reform. Seventh, regarding those with a sense of shame and remorse: they attain peace and security; should there be among the assembly of followers those who have lost their way toward the Path-mind and committed offenses, [the teacher will guide them].
Constantly harboring a sense of shame and fear, one reforms the past and cultivates the future;
seeking purification, one is further able to rescue and deliver others, becoming a place of refuge. Eighth, one cuts off present outflows and the evil that has already arisen.
Having thus eliminated [defilements] from the body, the mind becomes pure.

Ninth, one manifests the practice of *poṣadha* (the Uposatha) without deficiency or flaw; tenth, one severs future outflows (*āsrava*) so that unarisen evils never arise again, thereby ensuring that the True Dharma endures for a long time. Those who uphold the precepts act with personal purity.
Furthermore, one is able to cause others to uphold the precepts;
by means of the essential principles of the net-like discipline, one rectifies the multitude and benefits the times.
Through this process of transformation upon transformation, those who have fallen are raised up once more—this is among the ten benefits.
The first three rely on the assembly to seek liberation;
the middle six practices accomplish the dual benefit of self and others;
and the final one is able to cause the Three Jewels to flourish.
Only those who uphold the precepts obtain these ten benefits.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
among these ten benefits...
Regarding the meaning of these three sections:
the first three phrases clarify the attainment of benefit among the various dharmas;
the middle six phrases clarify the attainment of benefit within the dharmas of practice.
The final phrase clarifies that one gains benefit within the teachings.
Regarding the three types of assemblies mentioned at the outset:
the first clarifies the provisional-name Sangha of the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Because they are subsumed within the Vinaya teachings, they are included in the category of the Saṃgha;
hence it is said: "First, being encompassed by the Saṃgha.
Second, it clarifies the harmonious Saṃgha of internal ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
With one heart they uphold the Vinaya, taking harmony and compliance as their foundation; therefore it is said that these two things cause the Saṃgha to rejoice.
Third, the true Saṃgha of the noble stages is explained:
acting in accordance with the Vinaya, they do not conflict with or vex one another.
Therefore it is said that these three things bring peace and happiness to the Saṃgha.
Now, to clarify: if an external ordinary bhikṣu can maintain the precepts and remain pure in both what he sees and hears, he may enter into these three kinds of Saṃgha.
By participating in the same *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā*, one obtains these benefits of the communal Dharma.
Next, regarding the explanation of the ritual procedures (*caryā-dharma*) in six phrases:
the first two phrases clarify the maturation of those below.
This refers to the benefit for those within the ranks of the śraddhānusārin and dharmānusārin, who are ordinary persons in training.
The next two phrases clarify the maturation of the intermediate stage;
this refers to the benefit for the noble persons in training who belong to the Sangha of those on the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The latter two lines clarify the aforementioned maturation,
namely, the benefits of the qualities of the fruit of arhatship consisting of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The eleventh line clarifies the benefit of the teaching.
They bring others to maturity;
by preaching the Dharma and transforming beings, they bring benefit to the world,
perpetuating the true path so that it never ceases.
Therefore it is said that these ten [precepts] cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
To examine the intention behind the Tathāgata’s formulation of the precepts: they were originally not intended for those whose hearts are inherently evil.
It is precisely for this purpose that one seeks to open wide the true path to Nirvana,

so as to cause bhikṣus to practice in accordance with the Dharma and thereby attain the realization of the Way— the unsurpassed, eternally abiding, and forever quiescent state of rest attained by the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that for the sake of the bhikṣus, the ten points of meaning—the precepts of all Buddhas—have been compiled. 2.
Second, regarding the teacher and disciple, and the Dharma and its practice: the Upādhyāya (Preceptor) should possess ten qualities.
First, upholding the precepts;
second, being well-versed in the Abhidharma;
third, being well-versed in the Vinaya.
Fourth, training in ethical discipline;
fifth, training in meditative concentration;
sixth, training in wisdom.
Seventh, one purifies oneself from offenses and causes others to be purified from offenses.
Eighth, one is able to nurse the sick oneself.

Ninth, when a disciple encounters difficulties regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one is able to escort them away or send someone to escort them, thereby liberating them from those difficulties.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one who fulfills ten conditions may serve as a *niśraya-ācārya*; he should possess ten virtues: first, he must fully maintain the two hundred and fifty precepts;
second, he must be widely learned.
Third, he is able to instruct his disciples in the Abhidharma;
fourth, he is able to instruct his disciples in the Vinaya;
fifth, he is able to instruct his disciples to abandon wrong views and abide in right views.
Sixth, knowing the prātimokṣa precepts;
seventh, knowing the recitation of the prātimokṣa precepts;
eighth, knowing how to perform the poṣadha ceremony.
Ninth, knowing the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā*.

Tenth, having completed ten years [of seniority], the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) must possess ten virtues; these are also the same as those set forth in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Among the ten [types of] *ācāryas*, the *madhyama-ācārya* (intermediate teacher) should be endowed with five virtues: first, knowing the superior deportment, which is the purification of bodily and verbal precepts.
It is also called the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); knowing the second [truth] as the superior purification of conduct is the precept of pure mind.
It is also called the precept coexistent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*); knowing the third [truth] as the superior *prātimokṣa* precept is the precept of pure wisdom.

It is also called the "precept concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*); because it cultivates supramundane practices that far exceed mundane dharmas, it is termed "superior. Regarding the four types of *jñapti-karman*, this phrase refers to being well-versed in the monastic laws.

He is accomplished in literary expression; his speech is eloquent and sharp; he has completed five years of full ordination (five *varṣas*); he has studied the precepts for five years and established himself in their practice;

he is capable of performing *karmavācanā* rituals for others; and as an Upādhyāya or Ācārya who confers the precepts, he should possess these five virtues: first, he must be well-versed in the rules concerning obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*).
Second, being skilled in knowing the dharmas that are free from difficulty;
third, being skilled in knowing the dharma of making a formal announcement (jñapti);
fourth, being skilled in knowing the dharma of performing a formal act (karma).
One who possesses these five virtues—having pure conduct and observance of the precepts—is capable of leading the assembly.

Regarding the formal ritual for a teacher to accept a disciple, it should be endowed with five factors: first, if a disciple falls ill, the teacher should personally attend to them or dispatch someone to look after them.
Second, if a disciple does not find the dwelling place agreeable, he should provide a place for them to rest.
Third, if a disciple has doubts regarding matters, he should be able to resolve their mind in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, if a disciple gives rise to wrong views, he should be able to instruct them to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view.

There are five qualities by which a disciple should respect and honor their preceptor, for he is a refuge and a support equal to the Dharma Master. A disciple relying on a teacher should possess five dharmas: first, affectionate care, serving and supporting him with all one’s heart regarding both clothing and food;

second, reverent service using one’s physical strength, never daring to be disobedient or arrogant; third, a sense of shame and gratitude for the teacher’s kindness, realizing that the weight of the Dharma is heavy and difficult to repay; fourth, a sense of remorse and fear of his venerable dignity, not daring to commit transgressions; fifth, delighting in staying close to him to receive instruction and admonition, drawing near to him daily to learn of his virtues. There are five kinds of ācāryas.

First, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, who is the preceptor for the initial renunciation and the ten precepts; second, the *karmācārya*, who is the preceptor for receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*); third, the *śikṣācārya*, who teaches the observance of dignified deportment; fourth, the *vācanācārya*, who receives and studies the Dharma and Vinaya; and fifth, the *niśrayācārya*, who must be a *upādhyāya* from whom one requests instruction and admonition.
There are five reasons why one should not dwell without a *niśraya*: first, being unable to diligently cultivate the precepts of dignified deportment.
Second, one cannot increase pure conduct;
third, one cannot increase the prātimokṣa precepts;
fourth, if one possesses wrong views, one cannot abandon them and abide in right view.

Five cases where one who has not yet completed five years of *varṣa* may leave a teacher possessing the fourfold division of the Vinaya; five dharmas by which one loses reliance on a teacher: first, the death of the teacher; second, the teacher’s departure; third, the teacher’s suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*);
fourth, if the disciple... [text truncated].

If one resolves to leave the boundary, there are three ways to abandon the path: first, if the preceptor relinquishes the precepts; second, if the teacher does not grant dependence; third, if the teacher relinquishes instruction. Fifth, one must remain in the presence of the upādhyāya; if the upādhyāya accepts one, [one remains].

The ācārya should no longer require the disciple to request instructions; rather, the disciple should protect the teacher through two matters: first, by providing offerings of food and clothing; second, by protecting the teacher through the Dharma.
When the teacher hears that the disciple is proficient, [he should grant him further instruction].

One should use skillful means, gentle speech, admonition, and parables to provide guidance and understanding, encouraging the study of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). A teacher should sustain their disciples through two matters: first, by providing food and clothing; [the second being instruction].
Second, regarding the inclusion of days and nights by means of the Dharma:

there are ten instances where one should not perform prostrations when instructing those who have left the household life on the rules of etiquette and dignified conduct. These are: first, after defecating;
second, after urinating.
Third, the body;
fourth, shaving the hair;
fifth, preaching the Dharma.
Sixth, chewing the tooth-stick;
seventh, rinsing the mouth;
eighth, the time for eating.
Ninth, eating and drinking;
tenth, eating fruit. Furthermore, there are ten occasions when one should not perform prostrations: first, one must not prostrate before a stupa or an image;
second, while performing work.
Third, oil for the three realms of suffering;
fourth, recitation and chanting;
fifth, not wearing clothes.
Sixth, circulating the Six Classics between the upper and lower towers;
seventh, the transmission of the scriptures;
eighth, communal debate.
9. Washing the bowl. 10.
Applying eye medicine. [From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "Three times a day one should request instruction and admonition":
1. Requesting at dawn; 2. At midday.]
In the same way, one should inquire after the teacher’s well-being three times each day at dusk;
likewise for the three times of repentance;
and likewise for the teacher’s instruction three times each day.
If one does not [do so], one incurs an offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are five ways of instructing disciples: first, reprimanding a disciple for even a minor fault by speaking harsh words and urging them with diligent effort; second, subduing and provoking the disciple who has troubled the teacher, thereby subjecting them to disciplinary training; third, penalizing and expelling those who violate the monastic regulations.
Minor offenses result in punishment;

serious ones result in expulsion from the monastic community. Fourth, the practice of praise: one should offer commendation in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings. Fifth, the practice of joy: one should maintain a sense of gladness in conformity with the teacher’s instructions. Furthermore, there are five methods for instructing disciples: first, the regulation for those who have committed an offense.
2. Those who do not commit offenses are permitted [to remain].
3. If there is any deficiency in the Dharma—whether it be that which has been prohibited or that which has been permitted—one should address it according to the Dharma.
4. For those who repeatedly commit offenses, one should apply disciplinary measures and provide them with mindfulness.
Regarding the five true merits, there is praise and rejoicing; there are three grades of reprimand: first, for minor faults and slight transgressions, there is reprimand with gentle words;
second, for medium faults and medium transgressions, there is reprimand with moderate words.
[The disciples] spoke words that were superior, further superior, and transgressing the superior, and they rebuked [the teacher]. The Buddha said:
"If you wish to have many disciples, you must diligently instruct and rebuke them according to the Dharma.
Disciples must protect themselves from afflictions. Before rebuking a disciple, one must first possess three qualities: first, [the fault] must be present before one."
Second, the departure;
third, the speech: "I now reprove you," consisting of five phrases of the method of reproving.

1. What you have done is improper conduct that violates reason; 2. It is not dignified deportment, as your movements and pauses have lost their measure; 3. It is not the way of a śramaṇa, for it deviates from the cultivation of the Noble Path; 4. It is not pure conduct, as it defiles the minds of the virtuous and good; 5. It is not compliant conduct, nor is it the careful instruction of disciples.

These five things are not to be done. There are five methods for reprimanding a disciple: 1. "Go! Your offense merits expulsion from the monastery"; 2. "Do not enter my room! Your offense merits expulsion from the room"; 3. "Do not perform services for me, nor accept any provisions from me"; 4. "Do not come to where I am, nor accept my invitations for instruction and admonition"; 5. "I will not speak with you, nor teach you the sūtras and the Dharma. There are five matters for which a disciple merits such reprimand.

First, lacking shame (*āhrīkya*), one commits transgressions without regard for others; second, lacking remorse (*anapatrāpya*), one fears neither sin nor seeks repentance; third, one does not accept instruction and does not comply with admonitions; fourth, one performs improper conduct and frequently engages in contemptible matters; fifth, one lacks reverence for teachers and the Sangha, frequently intruding upon them with glaring eyes and angry expressions, harboring thoughts of disdain in the heart.

Because they have no fear or restraint, they revile [others]. There are five matters concerning the reviling of disciples that constitute a loss of the Dharma: first, reviling for the duration of one's life;
second, reviling until the end of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Third, reproaching a patient without looking after them;
fourth, reproaching someone who is not present;
fifth, reproaching someone without pointing out their transgression.
One should not do so. When a disciple has been rebuked, they should perform five things: first, they should abandon their current work;
second, they should abandon it and request instruction and admonition;
third, they should practice samādhi every day and seek repentance.
Fourth, one should not remain in the presence of another person. Fifth, one should not depart without having confessed one's transgressions.

There are four kinds of teachers: First, one who lacks the Dharma and lacks food and clothing; such a teacher need not be consulted before departing. Second, one who lacks the Dharma but possesses food and clothing; such a teacher must be consulted before departing. Third, one who possesses the Dharma but lacks food and clothing; although it is difficult, one should remain with such a teacher. Fourth, one who possesses both the Dharma and food and clothing; this constitutes a pleasant dwelling. Regarding the first two types of teachers who lack the Dharma, one should depart after having performed confession.

Regarding the latter two types of teachers, there are certain dharmas from which one must not depart for as long as life lasts; however, according to the *Sengqi lüshi* (Vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra), there are five ways in which a disciple may lose [the status of] a dharma-disciple and should repent before departing: First, one should say to the upādhyāya: "I am practicing according to the Dharma, yet you, Upādhyāya, do not know it."
Second, I do not know whether my own conduct is in accordance with the Dharma;
third, when another commits an offense, I abandon them and neither instruct nor reprimand them;
fourth, even if I myself commit an offense, I do not recognize it.
Fifth, if one commits an offense and repents, yet remains unaware [of the transgression], there is no benefit from the training of the renunciant life.

Therefore, when a disciple wishes to go abroad to seek instruction, observe, and study, the teacher should evaluate them according to three factors: first, whether the purpose of their undertaking is wholesome.
Second, the destination must be favorable.
Third, one should listen to whether the companions are suitable before proceeding.

If even one of these matters is unfavorable, one should desist. There are five types of persons whom the Saṃgha should not take as companions on a journey: first, those who delight in traveling too far ahead.
2. Walking behind when others are walking in front;
3. Interrupting the speech of others;
4. Not distinguishing between good and evil speech, nor praising or extolling good words while disparaging evil ones.
Fifth, having obtained profit in accordance with the Dharma, one does not accept it back from them at an improper time.
These five points should be taken as companions [in practice]. There are five qualities by which one should not form a close intimacy: first, if one delights in quarreling.
Second, if one performs many actions;
third, if one quarrels with a superior bhikṣu while sitting in the assembly;
fourth, if one delights in wandering about without ceasing.

There are five mental states in which one does not wish to preach the Dharma to others, yet speaks of good and evil to them.
