There are seven qualities by which one should form a close friendship: first, being able to give what is difficult to give, without begrudging wealth or treasures; second, being able to do what is difficult to do, without begrudging physical labor; third, being able to endure what is difficult to endure, without begrudging one’s mind or spirit, and without mutual resentment or anger; fourth, sharing secret matters with one another, expressing one’s feelings and speaking the truth without concealment or reservation; fifth, mutually concealing each other’s faults and protecting one another, without broadcasting each other’s transgressions; sixth, not abandoning one another when encountering suffering, tending to the sick, and rescuing and relieving one another in times of urgent distress; seventh, not slighting those who are poor or lowly, not following after power, not discarding others in times of decline, and not avoiding righteousness when seeing profit. There are ten virtues by which one should be appointed to instruct and admonish bhikṣuṇīs: first, being fully endowed with the precepts and well-cultivating dignified deportment.
Second, being widely learned and having skillfully cultivated an understanding of the sūtras and śāstras;
third, reciting the two divisions of the precepts and becoming thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya texts;
fourth, making decisive judgments without doubt and deeply penetrating the essential meaning.
Fifth, he is skillful in preaching the Dharma, with eloquent and lucid speech.
Sixth, having left the household life from a great clan, his conduct and principles are worthy of observation.
Seventh, his countenance is upright and handsome, and his deportment is dignified and refined.
Eighth, she must be capable of preaching the Dharma to nuns and be well-versed in discerning their spiritual capacities.
Ninth, she must not have violated the grave prohibitions and must be free from internal defilement.
Tenth, she must be at least twenty years of age and possess high virtue and great dignity.

The Bhikṣuṇīs must observe the Eight Rules of Respect: 1. They should pay homage to the body of a Mahābhikṣu; this is respect through physical action (*kāyakarma*). 2. They must not revile or slander a bhikṣu; this is freedom from fault regarding verbal action (*vākkarma*). 3. They must not bring up the offenses of a bhikṣu to cause him to be reminded of them; this is freedom from deceit and arrogance regarding mental action (*manaskarma*). 4. After two years of training in the precepts, they receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the assembly of Mahābhikṣus; the method for receiving ordination is established by the Mahāsaṃgha. 5. If they commit an offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṃgha (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), they must perform *mānatva* for half a month within both assemblies (the Bhikṣu and Bhikṣuṇī Saṃghas) to purify themselves of the offense. Since one should originally maintain these precepts firmly, having now violated this rule, [one must undergo penance].

Offenses are extinguished by the Sangha; this is the Dharma for the extinction of offenses. It is set forth that among the Great Bhikṣu Sangha, there is the practice of requesting instruction every half-month for those who have left the household life. To study the precepts is the foremost priority.

Please provide instruction on the seven points of conduct for disciples: one must not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no fully ordained monks; as the path of cultivation involves many difficulties, one must rely upon protection, seek counsel, and resolve doubts.
The sites for alms-gathering are located at a distance of one *yojana*— forty *li*— from the great monastic community;
one can travel to and from them on the same day.

If one follows the *Śrāmaṇera-śīla-vinaya*, it is permitted to travel as far as seven days' journey to and fro in order to fulfill the requirements for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*). Eighth: at the conclusion of the rains retreat, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) before the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) regarding three matters; many people are confused about this.
Yet those looking on clearly fear that they might inadvertently transgress or fail [in their duties] without realizing it;

thus, out of great compassion, [the Buddha] revealed this so that they would not fall short—this being among the Eight Points of Respect. Of these eight, the first three clarify the ritual for paying respect.
The middle two [sections] clarify the Dharma that is honored;
the final three clarify the method for requesting instruction.
The first [of these] concerns honoring others as one's teacher.
Next, one should take up the Dharma by relying on others;
finally, one should practice according to what has been taught. 3.
The Dharma of the Saṃgha. Regarding the third [section], entering the assembly, there are five dharmas. Indeed, one does not achieve goodness through solitary practice alone.
Since one stands in dependence upon the community,
one should carefully understand the laws of the community and accord with them with reverence.
Furthermore, once one’s own practice is perfected, one will be capable of being commensurate with the community.

Therefore, one must skillfully master the protocols for governing and investigating; in all matters, one should first give rise to a compassionate mind that loves and delights in the various dharmas, and only then enter among the assembly without any laxity.

1. One should not act in ways that cause discord or distress to the community; these two [faults] require one to humble oneself like a cloth used for wiping dust. 2. One should be modest and respectful, guarding against transgressions and never treating the assembly with contempt. 3. One should skillfully know how to sit and rise.
If one sees a senior elder (sthavira), one should not sit down;
if one sees a junior elder, one should not rise up, for the assembly must remain composed. When among the Sangha, one should not engage in miscellaneous talk or discuss worldly matters.

If one preaches the Dharma oneself or requests another to preach the Dharma, these five cases are based on the Dharma; however, if one sees something improper within the Saṃgha and cannot endure it in one's heart, one should remain silent.

There are five kinds of improper silence regarding the instigation of disputes: first, when a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the Dharma, yet one remains silent because one does not agree with it while participating in the ritual procedure.
1. When what is seen differs and cannot be resolved through discussion, one should request forbearance;

thus the harmonious assembly of the Dharma does not become divided. If one finds companions of like mind, one should remain silent and leave them to their own course. Having obtained assistance from others, one should not remain silent and tolerate what is contrary to the Dharma. 2. If one sees a minor offense and remains silent while allowing it to proceed, this may be called "covering over with grass" (tirokuṭṭa); yet to tolerate such defilement within the assembly is improper. 3. If one acts as a mediator for a *pārivāsika* (one undergoing probation) and remains silent while the Saṃgha carries out the three formal acts of suspension (*tajjaniya-kamma*, etc.), [this is likewise improper].
This is called "separate dwelling" (*pārivāsika*).

One may not participate with them in the same *dharmakarma* (ritual act). If five [monks] are on the boundary of the *sīmā* (precept field) and remain silent while intending to perform a *karmavācanā*, they should be summoned to assemble.

Fearing that the assembly might become incomplete and thus invalidate the act, there are five kinds of lawful silence: First, seeing another act unlawfully and remaining silent—since an unlawful *karmavācanā* ought to be protested and stopped.
1. Because expressing compassion at an inappropriate time would disturb the minds of the assembly; unlike those [who speak], one who has no fault regarding oneself [need not speak]. 2.

Because if one cannot find companions and remains silent while alone, it is useless for the assembly to declare one right. 3. Because if one commits a grave offense and remains silent while initiating a major matter, there is fear that the assembly will fall into disorder. 4. Because when residing together, remaining silent in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony prevents the arising of discord. 5. While on the grounds of communal residence, since all people have assembled, it is not appropriate for there to be conflict or disorder; when intending to adjudicate the affairs of another, one should first examine five things. First, examine whether the prior matter is factual or not.
The second observation is whether there will be benefit;
the third observation is whether now is the appropriate time; and the fourth observation is whether it is not [the case that it is inappropriate].
Does joining the Sangha produce defilement?
For the fifth time, one observes whether one has obtained good companions. Having observed these five dharmas, one should maintain a virtuous mind.

One who rectifies the assembly with wholesome thoughts and establishes regulations, who punishes evildoers and adjudicates legal disputes, should possess five virtues: 1. Having received the precepts purely, fearing transgression and possessing a sense of shame, one never distorts the principles of justice. 2. Being widely learned and having a broad understanding of both the words and their meanings, one cannot be defeated when tested or challenged. 3. Extensively reciting the two divisions of the *Vinaya*, one is skillfully able to recognize the rules for monks. 4. Being able to question and answer, and being able to provide instruction and reprimand according to the Dharma—including performing acts of reconciliation or expulsion—one is capable of bringing about joy and satisfaction, acting appropriately so that all find their due place. 5. Being highly skilled at extinguishing disputes and possessing many expedient means, one can harmonize and resolve the aforementioned matters. One endowed with these five virtues is fit to diligently manage the affairs of the Saṃgha as its general administrator. A *vinayadhara* (master of discipline) who adjudicates matters for others should possess five virtues: 1. Being well-acquainted with the characteristics of offenses.
Second, skillfully knowing the characteristics of non-offenses;
third, skillfully knowing the characteristics of light offenses;
fourth, skillfully knowing the characteristics of heavy offenses.

Fifth, one who possesses excellent knowledge and decisive judgment dwells without doubt in the *vinaya* and remains unshakable. One should possess these five virtues before being able to adjudicate matters for others or charge someone with an offense. A person should internally possess these five virtues: 1. Knowledge of the proper time: One does not bring up matters at an inappropriate time; rather, when it is appropriate to charge someone, one acts according to the occasion. 2. Truthfulness: One does not use falsehoods; having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], one does not wrongfully accuse another. 3. Beneficence: One does not act to cause harm or diminishment; rather, one causes the other person to reform their faults and turn toward goodness. 4. Gentleness: One does not use harsh or crude speech in exhortation and admonition; once the advice is given, there is no abusive language. 5. Compassionate mind: One does not harbor thoughts of anger or malice toward the other person, nor cause them fear or harm. If one does not deliberate upon these five factors, [one is unfit].
One must not lightly reveal the Way or speak of the faults of others, for this may cause disorder among the assembly, harm others, or distress oneself;

one must exercise profound caution. The abbot, the *karmadāna*, and the administrative officers should possess five virtues: first, they should be without attachment and impartial toward kin; second, they should be without anger and refrain from seeking retribution against enemies; third, they should be without fear and not intimidated by the powerful; fourth, they should be without delusion and not deceive the weak; fifth, they should know their own lot and be skilled in discerning matters both settled and unsettled. Since monastic affairs are of great importance and the benefits they bring are vast, [these qualities are essential].
If one can manage these affairs with a sincere heart and not shrink from the hardships of administration,
practicing them through five methods alone and seeking no reward or praise; this is what is meant.
One does not act for one's own sustenance,
nor does one encroach upon the benefits of others;
having done so, one does not rely on this to become self-exalting.
One should always cultivate a sense of humility and diligently make offerings to others;

those who can do so will be reborn in heaven as swiftly as an arrow shot. There are four kinds of Saṃgha: first, the Saṃgha of four persons, excluding [the assemblies for] the *pravāraṇā*, the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).

Second, in an assembly of five monks, all other matters that accord with the Dharma may be performed, except for the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
Third, in an assembly of ten monks, all [matters] may be performed except for the removal of offenses.

Regarding the four types of all other legal matters that may be performed by a community of twenty monks: there are three kinds of *karmavācanā* (formal acts). First, the *jñapti-karman* (motion), because the matter is easily understood through its expression. Second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion followed by one proclamation), because the matter involves deliberation. Third, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion followed by three proclamations), because the matter is difficult and requires careful, repeated resolution. The five types of illegal *karman* are as follows: first, the illegal *karman* of a separate assembly (*asamagrī-karman*), which is called "illegal" because it is not accomplished.

1. Because the monks within the boundary have not all assembled, it is called a "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-jana*). 2. An illegal concordant assembly where the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is not accomplished because the entire Saṃgha has not assembled together. 3. A legal separate assembly where the *karmavācanā* is accomplished despite the fact that the entire Saṃgha has not assembled together. 4. A case resembling a legal separate assembly where a *karmavācanā* is performed by analogy. 5. A case resembling a legal concordant assembly; furthermore, there is the practice of universal censure (*pratikrośa*).
Not only is the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) illegal;
one should perform a legal and harmonious assembly *karmavācanā*. There are three factors by which a *karmavācanā* is not accomplished: first, failing to perform the formal censure (*ukṣepa*).
2. Not performing the formal recollection (*smṛti*). 3. Not making a self-accusation.

Before performing a *karmavācanā*, one must first fulfill three requirements: 1. To raise the issue by exposing the person's faults; 2. To perform the formal recollection, asking, "Do you not recognize that you have committed such an act? 3. To assign the offense, wherein the person is fit to receive the disciplinary punishment. There are seven types of *karmavācanā*: 1. The *tarjanīya-karman* (reprimand), for a person who causes strife and discord among the Saṃgha.
Because there was a group within the community that did not protect [the offender],
this *karmavācanā* was performed;
this *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) involving two types of disciplinary punishment was carried out against this person who had corrupted and disturbed the *dānapati*.
It is not that one merely fails to protect others;
rather, because a layperson who has not yet gained faith ought to be made to believe, a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed to drive them away from the village.
Third is the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence): this refers to a person who has brought disgrace upon the community of monks.
Because he does not guard himself internally,

requiring him to train in the Vinaya and receive instruction; it is the *karmavācanā* of the four prohibitions against entering the homes of laypeople, as this person has brought disgrace upon the donors and will not reform externally.
This *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed because the lay follower who has attained faith should have their faith further increased;
it restricts that person from going in person and instead dispatches a virtuous individual to bring about reconciliation and apology.
Fifth, the *karmavācanā* for raising an accusation against one who does not acknowledge their offense: this person does not believe in the substantial reality of evil karma.
This is called the "view of causelessness.

Having performed this *karma*, the individual is suspended and cast out from the assembly, not being permitted to participate in monastic affairs. This is the *karma* of suspension for one who does not repent; such a person does not believe that karma can bring about its results.

When this *karman* is performed, [the monk] remains outside the assembly and does not share communal activities; because he does not relinquish these seven evil views, the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) is carried out against him. This is called wrong view.

Having performed this *karmavācanā*, one casts [the offender] outside the assembly and does not engage in communal activities with them; the four preceding *karmas* serve to discipline their lack of proper conduct.
The final three instances of formal accusation address those who lack faith.
Regarding those who "lack practice," it is said they have neither internal protection of practice nor external protection of practice.
Within the category of internal protection, they are disciplined through the *kukkucca-kamma* (reproach rite).
The *karma* for not protecting those who rely [on the Sangha] treats those who practice non-protection;
within external protection, the *karma* of banishment causes donors who have not yet developed faith and protection to do so,
while the *karma* of prohibition prevents them from approaching, thereby causing the faith and protection of donors who already believe to increase.
Therefore, there are four types of *karmavācanā*.
Next, regarding the "threefold suspension" (*tri-ukṣepa*):

and because afflictions act as conditions and aids, there is no instance of not abandoning [them].

Since suffering neither perishes nor remains,
and since impermanence does not seek cessation,
one should not raise the practice of "effortless application" within the study of the divergent paths.
Setting aside these seven methods of *karmavācanā* for disciplining persons, if one does not accept punishment, they should be disciplined by means of the *karmavācanā* of verbal abuse.

Regarding defilement through the monastery: taking the fruits, vegetables, and other items belonging to the Saṃgha and, according to one's own whims and desires, giving them to one family while not giving them to another family. A bhikṣu who commits these four offenses—

the latter two phrases constitute false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). The schism of the Saṃgha is accomplished through eighteen factors, which consist of nine pairs.

Six bases of wrong extremes.

by recording and identifying the matter, the dispute regarding non-offenses is settled.

One should request *kamma* from the Saṃgha to settle this dispute regarding the search for truth. This is the fourth method of settling disputes through *pātimokkha-thapana* (suspension of the recitation) and *paṭiññā-karaṇa* (formal admission), as well as the *vinaya* of "adjudication by others" (*tassapāpiyasika*) for indeterminate offenses.

then, by adjudicating the offense according to the Dharma, one extinguishes the dispute regarding the offense. Fifth, the *āpattisthāna-vinaya* is also called *āpattiparyeṣaṇā*.
When this person’s guilt was being assessed, their earlier words were not consistent with their later words.
The community of monks performed a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to discipline that person.

By subtly bringing forth the root of the offense, they extinguished the dispute through investigation (*mṛṣāvāda-vivāda*). Sixth is the *vinaya* of "majority decision" (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*), also known as "seeking the characteristics of the offense" (*bahumṛṣā-vādya*).
This person disputed the principles of the Buddha-dharma,
claiming that its meaning is vast and profound, beyond the comprehension of those of shallow knowledge;
he then extensively assembled great virtuous ones who were learned in the Dharma.
Investigating the Sūtras and Vinaya according to the Dharma, one takes the majority of voting sticks as the authoritative decision.

This is the "Bhūtamūla-vinaya" (the method of covering over with grass) for extinguishing verbal disputes: when the Saṃgha at a single residence is in mutual conflict and offense, such that they cannot be reconciled.

This refers to the settling of disputes through cessation. Among these seven methods of settling disputes, the first has a distinct essence but a universal application;

In protecting the Dharma, one must not conceal or shield [the transgression].
Furthermore, among the four types of disputes, each has its difficulties and its ease.

As for the second type of dispute, because the profound principles of the Mahāyāna are difficult to understand,

Disputes arising from searching for faults are settled by three methods:

First, there is the case where the person who searches for faults themselves possesses a transgression.
The person being sought is without fault;
therefore, one must recollect the *vinaya*.
Second, both the seeker and the sought may be at fault.
Therefore, the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict for one who was not deluded) is required.
Third, the person who seeks [the truth] is without fault,
while the person being sought has committed an offense.
Therefore, the *vinaya* concerning the locus of offenses is required.
As for settling disputes regarding transgressions, it is done by means of two methods of settlement.
He himself says he shall undergo the *trai-kuṭika* penance for covering the ground with grass.

he must undergo the *trai-kuṭika* penance by his own declaration.
Because one offense may involve a multitude,
it is necessary to cover the ground with grass;
thus, disputes over matters are settled by means of universal suppression.
When matters for settling disputes arise within a dispute over words,
yet one cannot tolerate [the other's position] and instead returns to disputing it,
one should settle it by means of either the presence of the parties (*sammukhavinaya*) or the majority vote (*yadbhūyasikīya*).
If, within a legal proceeding concerning a dispute arising from searching for the cause (*vitandā-vivāda*),
a matter for settling a dispute arises, and one does not accept it but instead returns to disputing it,

then one should settle it by means of the same methods used previously: namely, by means of mindfulness (*smṛti*), or by means of mindfulness, or by means of being undeluded (*amūḍha*), or by means of the locus of the offense (*sthāpanā*).
If a dispute arises from a case settled by "confession" (*pratijñā*), it is likewise settled by means of confession;
or if it arises from a case settled by "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*), it is likewise settled by covering with grass.
Having thus concluded these three types of disputes through the aforementioned procedures.

Because these seven methods of *vinaya* can extinguish the four types of disputes, they are called "extinguishing" (*nirghāta*). One confesses five *pātayantika* offenses before one pure monk by reciting the confession three times; one confesses six *duṣkṛta* offenses—here termed "evil deeds" (*āpatti duṣkṛta*)—before one pure monk by reciting the confession once.

Now, taking only the body to commit an act of *vaidharmya* (improper conduct), one performs it intentionally before another person and declares it once; this is the seventh type of offense of evil speech, which is equal to a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), consisting merely of speaking with the mouth to commit an act of *vaidharmya*.

Therefore, regarding the offense of *dukkaṭa* and *dubbhāsita* committed through mental action directed toward another person, if one has lost mindfulness and committed the offense, it is permitted to perform a *tajjaniya-kamma* (reproach) for the sake of repentance.

However, if one merely reflects within the mind and speaks the words aloud, resolving with a sense of shame and vowing never to commit the offense again, the sin is immediately extinguished. There are five rules for a junior monk to perform confession before a senior monk: first, to bare one shoulder.
Second, one must remove one's straw sandals;
third, one must bind the feet;
fourth, one must have the knees touch the ground.
Fifth, joining the palms and declaring the offense: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [name], have intentionally committed such-and-such an offense, though I do not recall the number of times."
I now confess and repent before the Venerable One;
I dare not conceal it.
Through confession, there is peace and happiness.
Without confession, there is no peace or joy;
by recollecting the transgression and revealing it,
one knows it and does not conceal it.
"Venerable sir, remember my pure body of precepts;
I am fully endowed with the purity of the *poṣadha*. This is said three times. The elder should say:

"Reproach yourself and give rise to a sense of weary detachment. He replies: "So be it. When the elder performs confession toward those seated below, there are four rules: first, bare the right shoulder.
Second, remove one's leather sandals.
Third, place the right knee on the ground.
Fourth, join the palms and confess the offense committed.
"Elder, please attend with one-pointed mind.
The text for the confession is as explained above.
The junior monk should speak as follows:

"Venerable sir, you should repent and give rise to a sense of weary detachment. He replied, "So be it. There are three kinds of persons who commit offenses: first, those who offend against the Saṃgha; second, those who offend against a group of many people;
and third, those who offend against a single person. There are three ways to perform confession.
Whether it be a Saṃgha,
a group of many people,
or a single individual acting as the master of confession for another, they should possess five qualities: first, they must be well-versed in the nature of offenses.
Second, being skilled in knowing the method of confession;
third, being skilled in knowing the purification through confession;
fourth, being skilled in knowing how to perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Fifth, one who is skilled in performing *karmavācanā*.

One who possesses these five virtues may accept the repentance of others and thereby eliminate their offenses. Regarding the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*): the first is the commission of sexual misconduct with a human male or female.
If it is among ghosts or spirits—
whether male or female— or among animals— whether male or female— in the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth,
it is likewise grave even when committed against another.
If one has already committed [the offense], it is likewise grave for another;
as with even a hair-tip entering [the boundary], a grave offense is incurred. Second, regarding the commission of theft: whether by robbery, by stealth, or by public officials forcibly seizing;
whether by burning, by legal means, or by harboring lustful intent.

Whether one acts oneself or instructs another to act, if one causes another’s property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more to be moved from its original location, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). Regarding the third offense, killing a person: this applies from the moment of initial entry into the womb.
As long as life has not yet been severed—
whether one kills by one's own hand or instructs another to kill,

regardless of what means are employed— if that person dies, one commits a transgression. Furthermore, to falsely claim to have attained superhuman states when in reality one is but an ordinary person, and to deceitfully say that one has attained the status of an Arya, constitutes a transgression.
Some say, "I have attained meditative concentration;
I possess the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds.

From the dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness upward, they speak of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four fruits of saintliness, the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and so forth.

Regarding the explanation to others of the eight grave offenses (*gurudharma*) of a nun: the first four are as explained above. As for the fifth offense, the violation involving physical contact (*sparśana*), it must involve a male; whether he is a child or an adult, provided he possesses lustful intent, the act constitutes an offense regardless of whether the person is a relative or a stranger.
Without distinguishing between monastics and laypeople,
both parties expose their bodies and touch one another;
from below the armpits to above the knees, if one approaches another, one commits an offense.
If he comes to you, you have also committed an offense.

It requires a lustful mind to receive the touch; if one feels pleasure upon being touched, it is an offense. There are six offenses and eight matters regarding the sin. Regarding the eight: first, with a lustful mind, a man takes hold of the hand.
2. Grasping the robe;
3. Entering a secluded place together;
4. Standing in a secluded place together.
Fifth, speaking together in a secluded place;
sixth, traveling together;
seventh, leaning one's body against another's.
Eighth, the common agreement.
Among these eight matters, there is no fixed order for offenses; one commits them according to circumstances.
If one fails to perform repentance for any of the seven matters, it constitutes a transgression.

If these eight matters are fulfilled, one commits a grave offense. Seventh, regarding the concealment of another’s grave offense: if one sees a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika offense, one should confess it before a single bhikṣuṇī.
If one intentionally conceals [a fault] and associates with those of evil intent, such that it passes the night until the following morning, one commits an offense.

If one fears being killed by another or that it would cause a schism in the Saṃgha, speaking of it does not constitute an offense. Regarding the eighth offense, which concerns the formal accusation of a transgression: if there is an evil bhikṣu...
The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (kamma) of the threefold accusation against him;
the person has been punished and has not yet repented,
and the Saṃgha has not yet revoked that formal act for him.
This bhikṣuṇī dispatched those who were compliant to provide her with support, forming a faction with the wicked and accepting what is contrary to the Dharma.
When the community of bhikṣuṇīs offered admonition, she stubbornly clung to her position and would not relinquish it.
The community of bhikṣuṇīs therefore performed the *karmavācanā* against her.

If one does not desist after three admonitions, one commits an offense; these are the six grave precepts for a śikṣamāṇā training in the six dharmas. First: no sexual misconduct. If one has already committed sexual misconduct, she may not proceed to receive the full ordination (upasampadā).
If one has physical contact with a man whose mind is deeply defiled, the precepts are deficient and one must receive the precepts again.
Regarding the two [precepts] against stealing: if one steals an object worth five *māṣaka* coins or more from another person, one is not permitted to proceed to the higher ordination (*mahā-śīla*).
If one takes four *māṣaka* coins or less, the precept is deficient;
one should receive the precepts again. Regarding the three [precepts], if one attempts to take a human life through expedient means but does not succeed, the precept is not lost.
If one intentionally kills an animal, insect, ant, flea, or louse, the precept is deficient.
One should further bestow the fourth precept of not lying: if one falsely claims to be an *arhat* to deceive others, they shall not be permitted to advance to the full precepts (*mahāśīla*).
If one has committed general lying, the precepts are deficient;

one should further bestow the precepts. Regarding the fifth precept of not drinking alcohol: if one drinks even a single drop out of a craving for its flavor when not suffering from a serious illness, the precepts are solely deficient.

One should instruct them to repent and then bestow the precepts again. Regarding the sixth [precept], not eating at improper times: if one has passed midday and thus broken the fast and violated the precepts, one should instruct them to repent and then bestow the precepts again. Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who uphold the prohibitive precepts would rather die than transgress them.
If one commits such violations, it is as if they had never originally left the household life;
they have brought ruin upon themselves and the Dharma,
and have brought disgrace upon their teachers and the Sangha.
They defile and bring disorder to the Three Jewels,
betray the fourfold kindness,
and fail to repay the offerings of the faithful; thus their transgressions are all the more numerous.
If one lacks the mind set upon the Path and merely wishes to do evil,
then one may indeed abandon the precepts;
however, one must not rely on the Buddha-dharma as a pretext for transgression.
If one wishes to relinquish the precepts,
one should kneel on the right knee with palms joined toward a bhikṣu who possesses the full precepts and say:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now relinquish the great precepts and return to being a layperson.
May the Venerable One bear this in mind.
"I am a white-robed layperson"—thus one should say three times. If one wishes to retain the five precepts, one should say:
"I return to being an upāsaka.
If one wishes to retain the ten precepts, one should say: [the same].
"I have returned to being a śrāmaṇera.
May the Venerable One remember that I am a śrāmaṇera."
"In the past, you received the precepts from the Saṃgha;
now, returning them to the Saṃgha according to your dharma,
the Saṃgha shall immediately bear witness to this."
If one is excluded from the *poṣadha* ritual, one is not permitted [to remain];
one must still stay within the assembly to participate in the communal Dharma activities.
By this principle, it follows that one cannot relinquish [the precepts] in the presence of others.
If a bhikṣuṇī returns [the precepts] to another bhikṣuṇī, she abandons the five ānantarya offenses: first, killing one's father;
second, killing one's mother;
third, killing an arhat.
4. Causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
5. With an evil mind, shedding the blood of a Buddha. The ten unwholesome karmas:
1. Killing. 2. Stealing.
Third, sexual misconduct;
fourth, false speech;
fifth, frivolous speech.
Sixth, double-tongued speech;
seventh, harsh speech;
eighth, covetousness.
Ninth is malice;
tenth is wrong view.
The first three constitute offenses of bodily action.
The middle four are offenses of bodily and verbal action;

the final three are offenses of mental action. Regarding the thirteen impediments (*trayodaśa-antarāyika*): first, the offense of a border-line transgression (*sīmāntika-āpatti*), which refers to one who has previously received the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*) and committed a *pārājika* offense.

If one has been subjected to the formal act of *parivāsa* (probation) for the sake of the Saṃgha, or if, after having abandoned the path, one subsequently wishes to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*), such a person is also difficult to admit into the order.

Because they remain outside the assembly, this is called a "borderline offense" (*antāpatti*). Second, regarding those who defile pure conduct: if it is a nun who defiles a monk of pure conduct, [the same applies].

Regarding those called "pure practitioners" (śīlavant): from the time they received the great precepts of renunciation, they have never committed sexual misconduct; thus they are named pure practitioners.

If one commits such [an act] while still a layperson, this pure practitioner is termed a "difficult-to-save thief. With a thieving mind, he receives the precepts; having no teacher, he steals the tonsure and dons the *kāṣāya*.
To participate in the *poṣadha* with others without having received the precepts,
or to perform formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*),
while harboring a thieving intent toward the Buddha-dharma, is called receiving the precepts with a thief’s mind.
If this refers to the six rules for śrāmaṇeras, nuns may likewise hear the *śīla* and the *karmavācanā* regarding theft;

they may also perform communal activities, yet they commit the four transgressions. As for those from internal or external paths, if such a person was previously an outsider who entered the Buddha-dharma and received the full ordination (*mahā-upasampadā*) but did not renounce their [former] precepts.
One who wears the *kāṣāya* yet acts as a non-Buddhist, whose mind of wrong views is heavy, will naturally lose their precepts;
if such a person later wishes to receive the full ordination (*mahānāsa*) within the Buddha-dharma, the precepts will not arise again. There are five types of eunuchs (*pañca-paṇḍaka*).
First, those who are eunuchs from birth;
second, those who are eunuchs due to physical deformity;
third, those who become eunuchs through coitus.
Fourth, the eunuch by transformation; fifth, the eunuch for half a month—these five types of persons have much affliction and lack the capacity to maintain the precepts.

Because their afflictive hindrances are heavy and they do not give rise to the Great Precepts, they are called "difficulties" [to ordination]. Sixth, killing one's father while still a layperson: at the time of killing, the father violates kindness and acts contrary to principle; this is a difficulty. Seventh, killing one's mother while still a layperson: at the time of killing the mother, one violates kindness and the offense is profound; one cannot receive the Great Precepts. Eighth, killing an Arhat while still a layperson: at the time of killing a realized person, the color of the body does not change upon death. Ninth, breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha by using the five kinds of false teachings to disturb the community’s mind.

He transformed and seduced those within the stage of ordinary practitioners (*pṛthagjana-śaikṣa*) to perform separate *poṣadha* *karmas*, thereby preventing the harmonious assembly of those who act according to the Dharma. He severed their practice of associating with the noble ones (*ārya*). Knowing this yet acting intentionally, he committed the tenth of the difficult-to-perform evil deeds: shedding the blood of a Buddha; this man intended to kill the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Buddha cannot be killed;
one merely incurs the grave offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
Yet, in the final age, there may be those who intentionally burn or destroy Buddhist temples, monasteries, images, or relics.

If one perceives an auspicious sign, it is equivalent to shedding the blood of a Buddha, which constitutes a grave offense (ānantarya). There are eleven types of persons who are not like ghosts, spirits, devas, or māras, yet may manifest as humans and undergo the ritual for receiving the great precepts (mahāśīla).
12. It is indeed difficult for those who are not human to receive [the precepts]; this refers to animals such as dragons, snakes, deer, or foxes that have transformed themselves into human form.
13. Those with two sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) are persons who possess both male and female organs.
They obstruct both the monastic and lay communities, leaving no place for them to be established. Among these thirteen obstacles, the first five are heavy affliction-obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the middle five are heavy karma-obstacles (*karmāvaraṇa*);
and the final three are heavy retribution-obstacles (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Within a single form, it cannot be altered.
If one has not yet received the precepts, one cannot receive them;
if one has already received the precepts, one cannot lose them.
One should not perform prostrations;
one should eliminate the assembly.
This is the classification of the three obstacles.
This is from the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
There is also a treatise stating that the first four [offenses] and the five *ānantarya* [crimes] [are included therein].
These nine are subsumed under karmic obstacles;
the one type of eunuch is subsumed under afflictive obstacles;
and the final three are subsumed under retributive obstacles.
The textual meanings differ;
one may choose and adopt according to one's own judgment.

Regarding the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there are four types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) corresponding to the specific offense committed: first, the granting of the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (probation for concealment), which involves performing the method of repentance for as many days as the period of concealment has lasted.
This is the remedy for the fault of concealing an offense.
If a nun has a companion and does not conceal [the offense], she is granted two days of *mūlaparivāsa* (probation from the beginning).
If this person commits a grave offense again while undergoing *parivāsa*, she must likewise request *mānāpya* from the Saṃgha; the procedure for returning is the same.

Starting from the first day is the commencement of the practice. Third, regarding the *mānatva* (probation) *karmavācanā*: if there has been no concealment, one directly grants this disciplinary method—the six-night penance for a *bhikṣu* and the half-month penance for a *bhikṣuṇī*.
Fourth, regarding the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation) *karmavācanā*: twenty pure *bhikṣus* [are required].
This offense arises within the Saṃgha;

a bhikṣuṇī may have it washed away and extinguished by means of the forty persons of the two assemblies. Regarding the eight matters concerning failing to inform before spending the night: (1) going elsewhere without informing regarding other matters; (2) performing the repentance in the interim; (3) if there is a cause or condition and one goes again to another monastery, one should inform the Saṃgha of that monastery.

If one does not announce [one's departure], one loses [the status of] a night [within the boundary]; if one goes beyond the boundary twice without announcing it, or if there is a valid reason requiring one to go outside the monastery, one must announce it.

On the road outside the monastery, except for monks who are traveling, if one does not announce it, one loses [the status of] a night [there]. If visiting bhikṣus arrive and do not announce it, or if there is space for more monks to come, one should immediately announce it.
One incurs the offense of losing one night’s stay if one fails to inform [the community] within four monasteries.
However, there is no offense if the traveler does not inform [the monks] when a guest bhikṣu passes through the large courtyard of a saṃghārāma in great haste.
If one travels slowly and leisurely, one should follow the procedure for seeking permission (*ārocana*).

If one does not seek permission and stays overnight, there are five faults. If one does not send a messenger to seek permission, and if one is personally ill, one should entrust another bhikṣu to seek permission on one's behalf.
When a monk knows he is ill, he must not inform [the community] himself.
If the assembly does not [attend], he shall lose his lodging; two or three persons may sleep in the same room, but a bhikṣu should stay alone in a small room.
A bhikṣuṇī may have companions. Seventh, when staying in a saṃghārāma where no bhikṣus are present, there must be one who has received the full precepts (mahāśramaṇa) to stay in the temple.
If one stays alone where there are no other bhikṣus for even one night, it constitutes a lapse.
When practicing *mānatta*, one must always stay overnight within a community of at least four monks;

if the number of monks in that place is insufficient, it constitutes a lapse of one night. Furthermore, regarding the assembly at the proper time and the assembly at the improper time: the "assembly at the proper time" refers to the time of the *poṣadha*.
Regarding those who assemble at an improper time: when others are performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*), this assembly should be informed.
If it is not so informed, the overnight stay is forfeited.
If one is practicing *mānatva*, one should announce it;

if one does not announce it, the overnight stay is forfeited. (2) Regarding the thirty-five matters of forfeiture: the first two concern five matters of forfeiture. First, one is not permitted to bestow the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon others.
Second, one must not receive dependence (niśraya) from others.
Third, one must not maintain śrāmaṇeras.
Fourth, one must not accept an appointment by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs.
Fifth, if one has been dismissed, one should not go [to the assembly]. Second, there are five things that are forfeited: first, one may not act as the *poṣadha* master;
second, one may not engage in questions and answers regarding the *vinaya* within the Saṃgha.
Third, one must not perform *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) within the Saṃgha.
Fourth, one must not be included in the deliberations when the Saṃgha adjudicates matters.
Fifth, one must not serve as a messenger for the Saṃgha. The third [set] consists of five things to be forfeited: first, one should not enter a village too early.
Second, one should not return at the close of day.
Third, one should associate with bhikṣus and should not associate with non-Buddhists.
Fourth, one should comply with the instructions of virtuous bhikṣus.
Fifth, one should not speak contrary words. Fourth, there are five things to be forfeited: first, one must not commit this offense again.
1) Others should not be committed either;
2) if one commits something similar to this, or something arising from this;
3) or if one commits something more grave than this.
Fourth, one should not find fault with the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).
Fifth, one should not find fault with the person performing the *karmavācanā*. These are the five things to be forfeited. First, one may not receive the sitting mat spread out by a virtuous bhikṣu.
Second, one must not accept water for washing the feet.
Third, one must not accept articles for washing the feet.
Fourth, one must not accept cloths for wiping sandals.
Fifth, one must not allow others to rub or massage one's body. Sixth, one is deprived of five things: first, one must not receive prostrations from virtuous bhikṣus;
second, [they must not] join their palms [in greeting]; third, [they must not] offer inquiries after one's well-being.

Fourth, one must go out to meet [the offender]. Fifth, one must not accept the robe and bowl held by a virtuous bhikṣu. Seventh, there are five matters that must be forfeited: first, one must not bring charges against a virtuous bhikṣu;
second, one must not perform the formal act of *smṛti-karman* (causing him to remember) or the *jñapti* (motion) on his behalf.
Third, one must not testify to matters concerning others.
Fourth, one must not obstruct another’s *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*.
Fifth, one must not engage in quarrels or disputes with virtuous bhikṣus. Among these thirty-five matters:
The first ten [points] deprive one of the virtues of a teacher;
the next ten deprive one of acting according to one's own will;
and the subsequent ten matters deprive one of the offerings and services [received].
Regarding the latter five [precepts], one must not interfere in the affairs of others; one should practice in accordance with this rule.

If one violates even a single item, the offense is not extinguished, and one may not be granted the *karmavācanā* for absolution from guilt. There are ten types of *sthūlātyaya* offenses by their very nature: first, eating human flesh.
2. To keep human skin;
3. To shave the hair from above the genitals and the hair from under the arms;
4. To use medicinal substances to irrigate the anal passage.
Fifth, wearing a *kambala* made of human hair;
sixth, practicing nakedness;
seventh, using a stone alms bowl.
8. Anger destroys clothing;
9. Anger destroys rooms;
10. Anger destroys temples and stupas.
In all such cases, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
For minor instances, one should perform repentance before a single person;
the ritual procedure is the same as that for a pāyattika offense.
Because this offense is more grave than a *duṣkṛta*, it constitutes the fifth category (*āpatti-skandha*).
Among these, there are also those that are particularly heavy,
such as eating human flesh raw or with malicious intent destroying a monastic dwelling or a Buddhist stūpa.
This refers to the confession performed by two or three people for offenses of the first two categories.
As for *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) of the first or second category, the Saṃgha performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for their confession.
This principle is derived from the *Mātṛkā*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"With a mind of anger, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense by destroying six kinds of things:
a bowl, the three robes, a stupa, a monastery, or a boundary."
There are three kinds of persons before whom one who has committed a *naiḥsargika* offense should relinquish it:
the Saṃgha, a group of many persons, or a single person. There are four kinds of false speech: first, false speech constituting a *pārājika*.
2. Saṃghāvaśeṣa lying; 3. Pāyattika lying; 4. Pratideśanīya lying;
5. Five kinds of stinginess: first, stinginess regarding material wealth.
Second, stinginess regarding dharmas;
third, stinginess regarding families;
fourth, stinginess regarding dwellings.
The five types of praise for stinginess; the five hindrances that shroud the mind: first, stinginess and greed;
second, ill will;
third, sloth and torpor.
Fourth is remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

Fifth is doubt (*vicikitsā*): the two hindrances of greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) can obscure the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), while the two hindrances of drowsiness (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) obscure the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
The single hindrance of doubt can shroud the category of wisdom. The ten afflictions of the fetters are: first, the view of a self-identity;
second, the view of extremes;
third, false views.
4. Adherence to views; 5.
Adherence to precepts and observances; 6. Doubt.
Seven are greed;
eight are ill-will;
nine are pride.
The ten types of ignorance.
These ten afflictions drive the mind into restless activity, causing it to flow and circulate without abiding.
By contemplating the principle of emptiness and non-self within the Four Noble Truths, one extinguishes the first five views and attains the practice of signlessness.
Next, by severing the remaining doubts, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The other four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm are classified into nine grades;
by exhausting six of these grades, one attains the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
By completely severing the lower three grades [of defilements], one attains the stage of Anāgāmin.
As the Sūtra says:
"By severing the three fetters, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna."
First, the view of self;
second, attachment to precepts and rituals; third, doubt.
These constitute three groups.
Furthermore, there are five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) in total:
first, restlessness (auddhatya).
Second, pride;
third, ignorance;
fourth, attachment to form.
The five [afflictions] of the formless realm are defilements;
these are the afflictions of the two higher realms,
which the Anāgāmin person has severed.
All have attained the fruit of arhatship. Regarding the three miserable realms and the four destinies:
first, hell; second, animals;

third, hungry ghosts—these are the three miserable realms, produced by purely evil karma. Fourth, the asuras, produced by mixed evil karma. As for the sentient beings of the six paths: first, the path of hell.
Second, the realm of animals;
third, hungry ghosts;
fourth, the realm of asuras.
The five realms of humans;

the six realms of devas. All three realms are suffering: first, the desire realm (kāmadhātu), from the hells above up to the six heavens; second, the form realm (rūpadhātu), from the Brahmā heaven of the first dhyāna up to [the highest heaven].
The four dhyānas comprise eighteen heavens; the three formless realms comprise the four heavens of emptiness, ending with the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.

5. Cultivating the Path and Practicing Wholesome Dharmas. Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva Constantly Practices the Six Mindfulnesses. 1. Mindfulness of the Buddha: His ten powers and fearlessnesses. One vows to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to Him. 2. Mindfulness of the Dharma: Its tranquility and cessation of all marks. One vows to read, recite, and contemplate its meaning. 3. Mindfulness of the Sangha: As a field of merit free from attachment. One vows to draw near to them and revere them. 4. Mindfulness of Precepts: Guarding against wrongdoing and restraining evil through the prohibitions. One vows to maintain them without transgression. 5. Mindfulness of Generosity: The ability to relinquish and abandon stinginess. One vows to practice it extensively for the sake of aiding others. 6. Mindfulness of the Heavens: Their purity and transcendence of worldly dharmas.
The unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood,
the state of secure abiding,
the heaven of the ultimate truth.

I now pray and seek that I may surely attain the supreme fruit; this is from the *Vinayottaragrantha*. Regarding the Six Recollections of a Śramaṇa: the first recollection is to know the month and day, and to know whether the current month is long or short.

Reflecting on how many days have passed, one contemplates the swiftness of impermanence; when the time for the *poṣadha* arrives, one reflects twice upon the number of years of the summer retreat, thinking: "In such-and-such a year, month, and day, at such-and-such a time, I received the full ordination."
I am now advanced in years with many summer retreats behind me and have no further business.

If I enter the assembly, I shall observe the proper order of seating according to seniority; furthermore, I have three invitations to consider. If I have already accepted a previous invitation, I now wish to accept this subsequent invitation.
"I shall now redirect the food previously requested for me to be given to the bhikṣu [Name].
That [Name] does not take it into account;
I have obtained food at my own discretion."
"Regarding that so-and-so who does not consider me [as his preceptor]:
he was previously invited as a donor. Fourth, one should maintain the three robes and perform the *śuddhika* (purification) rite for any surplus wealth.
Fifth, one must not eat separately from the community; when there are four or more people, all are considered eating separately from the community."
When eating, if there is a sick bhikṣu within the boundary, he should be treated urgently;
if not sick, he should follow the community in practicing the Path. There are five rules for a sick person: first, one must not eat what is unfit to be eaten.
Second, taking medicine with joy;
third, attending to the patient with truthful speech;
fourth, acting according to what ought to be done.
One should remain when it is time to remain.
Fifth, one is able to endure physical pain;

when the body has slight strength, one performs what ought to be done. Furthermore, according to the fifth phrase, one is able to purify seated contemplation. First, one reflects upon and repents of prior transgressions and afflictions.
This suffering is a retribution summoned by evil deeds;
if one does not repent, one will certainly fall into the evil realms.
This is because the remaining retribution for the sins accumulated in previous lives has not yet been exhausted.
From birth until now, from youth to old age,
my evil deeds have been many while my good deeds have been few.
I shall reflect one by one upon each of the precepts of the five categories.
Each of us has previously committed transgressions; we now repent them.
If one gives rise to this mind, the spirit will be born in a pure realm.
Second, one should contemplate the impermanent body as being composed of a provisional combination, like a clay vessel,
which quickly decays and is easily destroyed, incapable of being preserved for long.
If even life cannot be preserved, what is there to regret about wealth?
Do not take various garments and belongings to heart;
you should relinquish them without the need for formal entrustment.
After death, leave the matter to the monks; do not trouble yourself with lingering attachment or stinginess.
Third, one should practice the Buddha-recollection samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), skillfully regulating the breath, stabilizing the mind, and maintaining the meditative object.
Facing directly toward the west, one should visualize the pure buddha-field as if it were present before one's eyes.
In every thought-moment, like a flowing stream, one shall reach the other shore.
Furthermore, a sick person should measure their own condition by three factors: first, the severity of the illness.
If one obtains food and drink according to one's wishes,
or medicine for one's illness according to one's wishes and to one's liking, the attendant for the sick— whether these three things are obtained or not— [should remain attentive].
This illness will inevitably lead to death and cannot be cured;
once the retribution of impermanence has reached its limit, it cannot be saved.
At that time, the patient should make preparations for death.
Do not consume what is contrary to the Dharma, nor break your fast.
Second, regarding minor illnesses:
if you obtain food and drink according to your wishes.
Medicinal decoctions may be taken according to the illness and as one desires. If the caregiver does not contract the illness, they will not die;
by simply resting slightly, the illness will naturally subside.
At that time, a sick person must not, on account of their illness, desire to drink or eat in a manner that breaks the precepts or consumes alcohol.
Third, if one with a moderate illness is permitted to eat and drink according to their own wishes,
the illness will be cured.
If one does not recover from the illness, one will surely die.
At that time, the patient should reflect for themselves and consume [the medicine] according to what is appropriate for the illness.
If one is unable to exercise self-restraint,
the caregiver should provide moderation;
the same applies to the administration of acupuncture, moxibustion, and medicinal decoctions.
The same applies to seeking caregivers and providing them with necessities.
Furthermore, since a patient often experiences much distress and anger, one should practice self-discipline;
for it is difficult to endure even the sincere kindness shown by others when one is ill.
How much more so if one further adds harsh words to provoke them?
It would be of no benefit for me to look at them;
they might become discouraged in mind and no longer look at me.

I would then die. For this reason, one should feel shame before others, protect their feelings, and encourage them with praise. There are five things that a caregiver may obtain: first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat.
First, one may give what is edible.
Second, one does not defile it with the urine, saliva, or vomit of those who are lowly or ill.
Third, one possesses a compassionate heart and does not act for the sake of food or clothing.
Fourth, they are able to manage the medicinal decoctions,
until the patient recovers or even dies.
Fifth, they are able to preach the Dharma for the sake of the sick person.
One who suffers from combined illnesses delights in their own body and increases in wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). The Buddha said:
"When you were strong and healthy, you did not look upon the illnesses of others."
"You have now fallen ill;
who will attend to you?
He then addressed the bhikṣus.
For one who has left the household life,
failing to tend to the sick is of no benefit;
if one can provide for the sick, it is superior to making offerings to the Buddha.

Seeing suffering and impermanence with a heart of profound compassion is the foremost path of cultivation for attaining immeasurable merit. There are five benefits to chewing a willow twig: first, one’s breath will not be foul.
Second, it distinguishes flavors;
third, it digests the heat-aggregates;
fourth, it draws in food.
The Five Eyes’ Clarity: There are five dharmas for sweeping the ground that constitute great merit and virtue: first, not sweeping against the wind but with the wind;
second, one should not sweep with one’s back turned toward elders and superiors;
third, one should erase the tracks [of dust].

Fourth, clearing away refuse; fifth, returning the winnowing baskets and sieves to their original places. There are five benefits of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*): first, one is capable of traveling long distances;
second, one is able to engage in reflection.
Third, having little illness.
Fourth, good digestion.
Fifth, dwelling in the portion of virtuous concentration. There are five kinds of faults regarding the distracted mind’s faculty of vision: first, seeing bad dreams.
Second, the various devas do not provide protection;
third, the mind does not cherish the Dharma;
fourth, the mind is not fixed upon clarity.
There are five types of impure [sleep] and four kinds of improper sleep: first, the asura-sleep, which is lying on one's back;
second, sleeping while covering the ground;
third, the preta-sleep.
Fourth, sleeping on the left side. There are four types of lawful sleep: first, the lion’s sleep, lying on the right side with the feet one upon the other;
second, keeping the mouth closed with the tongue pressed against the upper palate.
3. With the right hand one holds the head, and with the left hand one follows along the body.
4. One does not abandon mindfulness, wisdom, reflection, and clear perception. There are five faults in facing the fire: first, it causes one to lose one’s complexion.
Second, it causes people to become weak.
Third, it causes people’s vision to grow dim.
Fourth, it causes people to gather in noisy crowds.
Fifth, those who speak much of worldly matters have five faults if they lack patience: first, they are fierce and intolerant;
second, they later feel regret;
third, many people do not love them.
Fourth, an evil reputation will spread. Fifth, one will fall into the evil realms after death. One should practice patience and cultivate the four modes of deportment:

First, the deportment of walking: advance straight forward with the body composed. Second, the deportment of standing: stand upright, keep the hands at the sides, and look straight ahead. Third, the deportment of sitting: sit cross-legged with knees firm, the body straight, and the eyes cast downward. Fourth, the deportment of lying down: lie on the right side with one foot resting upon the other, the body slightly bent, maintaining mindfulness and the thought that one shall rise early to practice. As for the four modes of verbal deportment: First, one should employ speech that is Dharma-consistent and truthful.
Second, one should practice right speech and straightforward speech.
Third, one should constantly practice harmonizing speech and speech that extinguishes disputes.
Fourth, one should constantly practice gentle speech and speech that gladdens the heart and is pleasant to hear. One should also cultivate the twelve dhūta practices.
*Thau* means few desires;
*tho* means contentment.
Because one shakes off afflictions and is free from attachment and clinging, it is called *thau-tho*.

What are the twelve? First, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*): this person does not accept robes offered as gifts or material gains. Second, wearing the three robes (*traicīvarika*): this person does not keep extra clothing or wealth. Third, wearing the [extra] robe according to need (*nāmatika*): this person keeps only what is necessary for the body and does not accumulate surplus items. Fourth, always begging for food (*paiṇḍapātika*): this person accepts invitations but does not eat food provided by the Sangha. Fifth, eating in a single mouthful (*khalupaścādbhaktika*): one eats only once and does not take further portions. Sixth, eating in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*): having finished the meal, one does not eat again even if the decorum is broken. Seventh, not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite (*khalu-paścād-bhaktika*): eating morning congee and midday rice, one does not take a second formal meal. Eighth, sitting at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*): observing that trees arise from the causal conditions of all phenomena.
My own body is likewise thus.

Ninth, sitting among the burial mounds, one contemplates the impurity of corpses and the impermanence of white bones. Tenth, sitting in the open air, one contemplates that all phenomena are empty and non-existent. Eleventh, sitting wherever one may be, one contemplates that all phenomena are in flux and lack any fixed nature.
Because of the lack of self-mastery, there is no self;

this is also following the name of tranquility as the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) practice. [One should] constantly sit and not lie down for twelve years, observing that sleep leads to indolence and that death results in falling into the evil realms.
If one does not straighten the body and rectify the mind, practice cannot be accomplished. These twelve items consist of three for wearing robes,
four for the rules of eating,
and five for sitting places.
The practitioner has no mental attachment to clothing, food, or dwelling;
yet, by relying on these conditions to give rise to the Path, they practice with ever-increasing diligence—this is asceticism (*dhūta*).

Regarding the various names for this in the Sūtras and Śāstras, let us present one explanation: practicing the five gates of dhyāna. First, for those with an abundance of sensual desire, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is prescribed.
Second, those with an abundance of hatred should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*).
Third, those with an abundance of delusion should practice the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*).
Fourth, those with an abundance of attachment to a self should practice the contemplation of the emptiness of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu-śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).

For those with a predominance of discursive thought (*vitarka*), one practices the meditation on inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) and the sixfold gateway dhyāna (*ṣaḍdvāra-dhyāna*). Regarding the counting: for those with cold-natured illnesses, one counts the exhalations;
for those with heat-natured illnesses, one counts the inhalations.
Directing the mind toward the bridge of the nose at the opening,
calmly and slowly count from one to ten; when the breath is mastered,
this constitutes one unit of thought.

If one deviates, becomes confused, or increases or decreases [the count], all such actions are improper. Second, following the mind and the breath as it enters and exits, one exhausts the root of the breath until reaching the state of no-mind, which is the gate of repentance. Third, the cessation of conditions: the mind remains still and dwells, guarding the tip of the nose at its opening.
Do not allow [the breath] to rush or scatter; observe the four directions and perceive the length and shortness of the breath.

Contemplate the breath pervading the entire body, seeing the vital energy (prāṇa) exiting through the pores like beads threaded on a string. Fifth, turn back and focus the mind upon the mental factors (caitasika).
Observe the mind with the mind.
If the mind takes other objects as its conditions, it is entirely in a state of agitation and distraction;

therefore, condition it so that it returns to abide [in stillness]. When the six sense-bases are purified and the mind is clarified, it remains on a single object without further agitation or distraction.
Upon entering the samādhi of the pure mind, eight kinds of unwholesome thoughts become manifest: first, thoughts of sensual desire;
second, thoughts of ill will;
third, thoughts of harm.
4. The perception of immortality;
5. The perception of relatives; 6.
The perception of one's native land.
Seventh, the thought of contempt;
eighth, the thought of lineage.
One who frequently contemplates these eight matters should practice the method of counting the breaths. Eighth, moving contact and light contact.
The sensation of heaviness,
the sensation of itching,
and the sensation of pain.
The sensation of roughness,
the sensation of smoothness,
and the sensation of cold.
The sensation of heat.
When these eight sensations arise and impinge [upon the senses], the precepts can either give rise to meditative concentration or give rise to affliction.

Regarding the three methods for training the mind as antidotes to eliminate [faults]: first, if the mind becomes agitated due to excessive diligence, one should focus the mind on its object and not allow it to wander.
Second, if the mind becomes sunken after maintaining the object for a long time...
One should employ skillful means to exert oneself and give rise to the mind;

third, having abandoned [extremes] and attained equilibrium, one should enter the samādhi of emptiness with right mindfulness and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness: first, contemplate the impurity of the body from head to foot, wherein the thirty-six components are all impure.

First, contemplate that the pus-filled sac is foul-smelling and filthy, like a dead snake or a dead dog. Second, contemplate that sensation is suffering: the fleeting pleasures of the world ultimately lead to ruin and destruction, and their oppressive nature is contrary to the mind;

thus, all such sensations are indeed the sensation of suffering. Third, contemplate that the mind is impermanent: the six consciousnesses arise and perish from moment to moment; the preceding mind is not the succeeding mind.
Like flowing water, a lamp, or a flame, one thus knows that human life is impermanent.

Through these four contemplations, one realizes the mark of non-self in phenomena; the mind grasps at provisional dharmas which lack reality, and the mind’s activity in creating karma is like an illusion.
All that is done is false and lacks any solid substance;
the phenomena that are the objects of focus are all empty. One cultivates the four right efforts: first, by skillful means, one prevents unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen from arising.
Second, one employs skillful means to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen.
Third, one employs skillful means to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
Fourth, one employs skillful means to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to increase and flourish.
Evil arises from the mind and is extinguished by the mind;
goodness arises from the mind and is cultivated by the mind.

One should diligently observe these four dharmas with a focused mind and cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). First, cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), mindful of all sentient beings and wishing to bestow happiness upon them.
One contemplates providing immeasurable clothing, food, and other necessities to sentient beings, bestowing supreme happiness upon them all equally, whether they be enemies or kin;
this is called the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Second, one cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*), mindful of all sentient beings and desiring to uproot their suffering.
This is called the threefold cultivation of compassion; the threefold cultivation of sympathetic joy consists of recollecting all sentient beings:
"If there are those who cultivate goodness, I shall praise and rejoice in them;
if there are those who commit evil, I shall exhort them to abandon that evil."
One should suppress evil and promote good, cultivating the mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings with complete impartiality.

Seeing neither enemy nor kin, one regards them as equal to the dharma of emptiness. One cultivates the six subtle practices: first, regarding consciousness, do not associate with form; clearly observe blue, yellow, red, and purple.
1. The mind is not stained by attachment; one practices sublime conduct and attends only to the two ears. 2. The ears do not cling to sounds, but take only the Dharma from beneath the words.
3. One does not crave or become attached to vocal sounds. 4. The nose is not stained by fragrances.
Fourth, the tongue does not crave flavors.
Fifth, the body does not cling to tactile sensations such as smoothness and so forth.

Sixth, the mind does not contemplate unwholesome dharmas. The five pure virtues of a śramaṇa are: first, generating the resolve to leave secular life in order to break away from worldly attachments and embrace the Way.
Second, they destroy their physical beauty by donning the robes prescribed by the Dharma;
third, they sever all ties of affection forever, remaining impartial toward kin and strangers alike;
fourth, they cast aside their very lives to honor and follow the Way.
Fifth, the aspiration to seek the Mahāyāna for the purpose of delivering sentient beings;
from the *Fuchian jing* (Sutra on the Field of Merit).

Section Six: The Dharma for Developing the Requisite Conditions for the Path. Regarding the sixth [section], "The Dharma for Developing the Requisite Conditions for the Path": desiring to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
One should practice the Dharma of the śramaṇa;
clothing and food shall sustain one's life,
whether coarse or refined, according to what is common to the community.
The Four Reliances: First, reliance on rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*).
This refers to those of superior capacity who take discarded items and use them as robes, rather than accepting offerings of faith.
This discipline involves having few desires so as to obtain what is necessary for the body and to cultivate the Way.
Those of middle capacity are unable to endure listening [to the Dharma] and thus receive shared property according to the order of the Sangha.

Those of lower capacity are permitted to receive individual offerings and the two types of robes—those obtained from the sale of valuables or those made from torn cloth—and they rely on begging for food. As for these people of superior capacity, they eliminate pride, humble their bodies, and subdue greed while begging for food.
One does not accept invitations for offerings,
nor does one discriminate between the poor and the wealthy;
rather, one seeks only what is necessary to sustain the body and preserve life in order to cultivate the Way.
Those of middle capacity are permitted to receive offerings according to the monastic order and to accept offerings for the purpose of sending them to others;

those of lower capacity are permitted to receive the monastery's standing provisions (*saṃghika-sthiti-bhakta*) and offerings made through special invitations. Third, regarding sitting at the foot of a tree: these are persons of superior capacity who do not accept rooms, bedding, seats, or robes.
Those of the lowest grade practice the Way by dwelling among burial mounds or under trees, obtaining only enough shade to conceal their bodies from view.
Those of the middle grade reside in small huts or stone chambers;
when they rise, their heads do not strike the ceiling, and when they sit, their knees barely find room.

Those of inferior capacity may listen to and receive [teachings on] large and private dwellings. As for the fourth reliance, the medicine of decayed substances: those of superior capacity, when ill, may consume this discarded medicine in order to eliminate the obstacle of karmic retribution.
This method of ingesting excrement and urine can cure various illnesses without harming the person;
one merely takes it to alleviate afflictions, preserve the body, and cultivate the Way.
Those of middle capacity receive ghee, oil, and honey according to the monastic order.
When a person of inferior capacity receives alms, the bhikṣu relies upon these four dharmas to sustain his body and maintain his life,
so that he may dwell in the cultivation of the Path.
Clothing serves as an external support.
Food serves as internal sustenance;
bedding and seating ward off external afflictions;
and medicinal decoations eliminate internal ailments.
Externally, one relies on clothing and shelter;
internally, one depends on food and medicine.
Only by means of these four conditions can one cultivate the Path.
Because they are able to give rise to the untainted (anāsrava), they are called the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
A bhikṣu should act according to his own capacity, practicing in accordance with the superior, middling, or inferior grades, and must not exceed his allotted portion.
Furthermore, if one of superior capacity practices inferior dharmas, they will regress;
if one of middling capacity practices superior dharmas, they will transcend them;
if one of inferior capacity practices middling dharmas, they will fail to reach them. The three robes and six requisites are: first, the *antarvāsa*, the five-strip *kāṣāya* robe.
One long, one short, and one heavy:
these are for the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).

When performing tasks such as defecating, urinating, washing the bowl, sweeping the ground, or other work, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*), the two-layered *uttarāsaṅga*, and the seven-strip *kāṣāya*.
Two pieces long and one short, doubled over and cut into strips;
this is the robe for entering the assembly.
When the community gathers for the morning or evening meal, for walking meditation, or for performing Dharma rites, one should wear the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*).
The method for attaching the hooks and measuring the fine dimensions is as explained below. This third [robe], the *saṃghāṭī*, is the garment worn when entering royal palaces or village settlements.
One wears the *mahākaṣāya* (great robe) when subduing celestial Māras, taming non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or transforming wicked people;
it may also be worn during moments of solemnity or when dealing with the unworthy.
One wears the *mahākaṣāya* when begging for food, receiving offerings, or entering a great assembly.
Robes of nine, eleven, or thirteen strips are considered inferior;
those of fifteen, seventeen, or nineteen strips are considered middling.
The twenty-first, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth [rules] constitute the superior grade.
They consist of three long strips and one short strip, triple-layered;
